revisions.scope: Anhua dark tea style kit
revisions.text: Anhua tea is kept for years and said to improve: the liquor turns redder and the taste sweeter and mellower, with a fuller scent. No agreed count of years marks it as aged. Keep it clean, dry and aired, away from mould and other smells.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Anhua dark tea kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Anhua dark tea style kit
revisions.text: In a small pot or gaiwan, use water at the boil and start with a steep of about 15 to 30 seconds, a little longer each round. Pressed and aged Anhua tea is also commonly simmered in a pot.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Anhua dark tea kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Anhua dark tea style kit
revisions.text: Pine smoke or pine resin above all, a sweet taste and aftertaste, and a mellow, thick, smooth cup; a liquor from yellow and orange to orange-red. Young tea is often smokier in the first infusions and a little bitter, sweetening as the infusions go on.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Anhua dark tea kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Anhua dark tea style kit
revisions.text: Anhua dark tea comes from Anhua County, a mountain county on the Zi river in north-central Hunan, under the city of Yiyang. Its name is a protected origin product in China, so it is tied to a defined place of making. Anhua is widely named as the main home of dark tea in China, and as a starting point of the old tea routes to the north-west.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Anhua dark tea kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Anhua dark tea style kit
revisions.text: Anhua teas come in three shapes. The three tips are loose teas, lightly pressed into bamboo baskets: Tianjian from the most tender leaf, Gongjian in the middle, and Shengjian, the coarsest, with the most stalk. The pressed bricks are Fu, Hei and Hua brick; Fu brick is the one grown on purpose with golden flower, in a warm, humid room for some weeks before it is dried hard. The flower rolls are tall columns pressed by hand inside a woven bamboo basket lined with leaf, named by their old weight in liang: Qianliang, a thousand, Bailiang, a hundred, and Shiliang, ten. Huajuan, flower roll, names the whole family and is also a nickname of Qianliang.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Anhua dark tea kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Anhua dark tea style kit
revisions.text: The raw leaf is sorted into numbered grades, and each finished tea is made from the grade that suits it, the most tender leaf going into the finest loose tips.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Anhua dark tea kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Anhua dark tea style kit
revisions.text: Anhua became a county in 1072, in the Northern Song, and tea from the area is mentioned from the Tang on, though as tea from the place, not yet as dark tea. In 1595, in the Ming, Anhua tea became an official tea, sold to the north-west. In the Qing, Shanxi merchants and others took over the border trade, and the loose tips and the large rolls grew out of that trade; the rolls are a Qing product, not a Ming one. Fu brick was first made in Anhua itself in 1953, at the Baishaxi factory, after Fu bricks had long been pressed in Shaanxi from Anhua raw tea.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Anhua dark tea kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Anhua dark tea style kit
revisions.text: Every Anhua tea starts as one raw tea, heimaocha, made from large Anhua leaf. The leaf is fixed, rolled, piled, rolled again and dried over a wood fire, and in Anhua that fire burns pine. The pine fire gives the tea its smell of pine smoke or pine resin, which sets it apart from dark teas dried another way; some newer lines dry by machine instead. The raw tea is then steamed soft and pressed: lightly for the loose tips, in moulds for the bricks, and by hand for the rolls.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Anhua dark tea kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Anhua dark tea style kit
revisions.text: A redder liquor, a sweeter, mellower cup, and sometimes a medicinal or herbal note.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Anhua dark tea kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Anhua dark tea style kit
revisions.text: A roll is packed into its basket and pressed tight by treading and twisting with long bars, then left to dry slowly in sun and night air for weeks rather than in a dryer. Rolls are usually kept whole to age, and reach drinkers later as slices, discs or small cut pieces, since a whole roll is far too big to buy or brew.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Anhua dark tea kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: banzhang
revisions.text: Prices for fresh leaf and finished tea rose steeply from the early 2000s, and the village became one of the best known names in pu’er.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian on the Wisdom Base Places review page, 2026-11-27

revisions.scope: banzhang
revisions.text: Most of what the trade writes about Banzhang describes raw tea. Ripe cakes with Banzhang in the name do exist, but they are less common than raw ones, and the name is seldom backed by a stated leaf source. Reading Banzhang on a ripe cake as the village itself is not safe. It more often points to a Bulang style of ripe tea, thicker in body and stronger than a plain Menghai blend.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian on the Wisdom Base Places review page, 2026-11-27

revisions.scope: banzhang
revisions.text: Banzhang is known for raw pu’er from old trees. The trade describes it as strong and bitter at first, then quickly sweet, with a long aftertaste and a heavy body. It is one of the most expensive named villages in pu’er, and Lao Banzhang is often called the king of raw pu’er.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian on the Wisdom Base Places review page, 2026-11-27

revisions.scope: banzhang
revisions.text: Xin Banzhang means New Banzhang. It was founded by people who moved out of the old village. The two are priced very differently, with Lao Banzhang far higher. Sellers say Xin Banzhang is less bitter, but too few places agree on that to treat it as settled.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian on the Wisdom Base Places review page, 2026-11-27

revisions.scope: banzhang
revisions.text: Banzhang on a label is a market name, and it is not proof that the leaf came from the village. The village makes a small amount of tea, and its name sells at a high price, so fakes and blends are widely reported. Some cakes sold under a Banzhang name blend in leaf from other Bulang villages. Lao Banzhang, Xin Banzhang and the wider Banzhang name are three different claims, and a label rarely says which one is meant.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian on the Wisdom Base Places review page, 2026-11-27

revisions.scope: banzhang
revisions.text: Banzhang is a group of tea villages inside Bulang Mountain, in the south of Menghai County in Xishuangbanna, Yunnan. The name covers more than one settlement. Lao Banzhang is the old village. Xin Banzhang is a separate village that grew out of it. Altitude is quoted differently from place to place, mostly between about 1,600 and 1,900 metres.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian on the Wisdom Base Places review page, 2026-11-27

revisions.scope: bulang-mountain
revisions.text: Bulang is a pu’er area whose fame is recent. Its reputation grew with the rise of Banzhang, whose price pulled attention to the whole mountain.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian on the Wisdom Base Places review page, 2026-11-27

revisions.scope: bulang-mountain
revisions.text: Bulang leaf is also used for ripe pu’er, and ripe cakes and loose tea sold under the name Bulang Mountain are common. The raw tea is strong, so ripe tea made from it is described by sellers as thick and full. Sellers disagree on whether it stays bitter after piling, so ripe Bulang tea is better judged cup by cup than from the name.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian on the Wisdom Base Places review page, 2026-11-27

revisions.scope: bulang-mountain
revisions.text: Bulang Mountain is known for raw pu’er from old tea gardens. The trade describes the tea as forceful: a strong, bitter start that turns sweet, thick liquor and a strong feel in the throat. It is often set against the softer, sweeter style of Yiwu. Villages differ a good deal. Lao Man’e is known for bitterness, and some other villages make sweeter tea.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian on the Wisdom Base Places review page, 2026-11-27

revisions.scope: bulang-mountain
revisions.text: Bulang Mountain on a label is a broad market name. Leaf from smaller or less famous villages is often sold in bulk, blended, and offered as Bulang tea. A cake called Bulang Mountain rarely names the village, and some makers do not state where the leaf came from. It points to a mountain style more than to one place.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian on the Wisdom Base Places review page, 2026-11-27

revisions.scope: bulang-mountain
revisions.text: The mountain takes its name from the Bulang people, who have grown and drunk tea here for a very long time. Lao Man’e is often described as one of their oldest villages, at about fourteen hundred years. Hani villages such as the Banzhang settlements sit in the same mountains.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian on the Wisdom Base Places review page, 2026-11-27

revisions.scope: bulang-mountain
revisions.text: Bulang Mountain lies in the south of Menghai County in Xishuangbanna, Yunnan, next to the border with Myanmar. It covers roughly one thousand square kilometres and is one of the larger tea areas in the county. It is a mountain area with many villages, not a single village. Banzhang, Lao Man’e and Manxinlong are among its named tea villages.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian on the Wisdom Base Places review page, 2026-11-27

revisions.scope: Phoenix Dancong style kit
revisions.text: Freshly roasted Dancong is rested for some months before it is at its best; how many months is not agreed. Keep it sealed, dry, cool and out of the light.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Phoenix Dancong kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Phoenix Dancong style kit
revisions.text: Dancong is sorted and sold by its aroma type, named for a flower, fruit or spice the scent recalls. The scent comes from the bush and the making, not from anything added: an orchid or almond Dancong names a smell, not an ingredient. The trade speaks of the ten aroma types. Nine names turn up in every full list: Huangzhi, yellow sprig; Zhilan, orchid; Milan, honey orchid; Yulan, magnolia; Xingren, almond; Jianghua, ginger flower; Guihua, osmanthus; Yelai, night-blooming flower; and Rougui, cinnamon. The tenth is most often jasmine.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Phoenix Dancong kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Phoenix Dancong style kit
revisions.text: Brew it gongfu style in a small gaiwan or clay pot, with about 3 to 8 grams for 100 to 120 ml and hot water, about 88 to 100°C; Chinese accounts mostly say 95 to 100°C. A quick rinse is common. Steeps start at a few seconds and grow a few seconds each round, and a good Dancong gives about eight to fifteen. Too long, too hot or too much leaf and it turns bitter and astringent.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Phoenix Dancong kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Phoenix Dancong style kit
revisions.text: Flowers above all, a sweetness that comes back after swallowing, a high scent that lasts, honey, often ripe fruit such as peach, and what the trade calls mountain rhyme, shan yun; a liquor from golden to orange-red or amber.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Phoenix Dancong kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Phoenix Dancong style kit
revisions.text: Phoenix Dancong is the oolong of Phoenix Mountain, Fenghuang Shan, in Chao'an, Chaozhou, in eastern Guangdong. Wudong is the peak named most often as its heart. The dry leaf is a long strip, twisted tight, dark and glossy, not rolled into a ball.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Phoenix Dancong kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Phoenix Dancong style kit
revisions.text: The old tea of the mountain was called bird-beak tea, and later Shuixian. Dancong is the everyday tea of Chaozhou, and gongfu brewing is tied to Chaozhou, where Chaozhou gongfu tea is still made with small vessels, set ways of pouring, and three cups.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Phoenix Dancong kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Phoenix Dancong style kit
revisions.text: The leaf is withered in the sun and cooled indoors, then shaken and rested in rounds; this is the step that bruises the leaf edge and builds the scent. It is fixed fast at high heat in a hot pan or drum, rolled into strips, dried, and roasted again as it is refined, sometimes over more than one round. Charcoal is the traditional fire. The roast is a main difference between teas: a light roast keeps the floral scent bright, a heavier one gives a deeper, sweeter cup with caramel in it.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Phoenix Dancong kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Phoenix Dancong style kit
revisions.text: Mi Lan Xiang, honey orchid, is one of the traditional ten aroma types and one of the most widely made, often named as a good first Dancong. It is described as honey-sweet with an orchid scent, with a cooked sweet potato note, and a liquor from golden amber to orange-red, depending on the roast. The one name covers a range of teas.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Phoenix Dancong kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Phoenix Dancong style kit
revisions.text: Dancong means single bush: the leaf of one bush picked and made on its own, never mixed with others. The bushes are chosen from the old Phoenix Shuixian plants of the mountain. Today a named Dancong is mostly grown from cuttings or grafts of a chosen bush, so one name no longer means one tree, though some very old trees are still made on their own.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Phoenix Dancong kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Phoenix Dancong style kit
revisions.text: Old bushes, laocong, are prized for depth and a lasting sweetness, and give little leaf; no age is agreed for when a bush counts as old. Song variety, songzhong, is a market label for the oldest named lines, Huangzhi above all, not a proven age. A legend gives the old trees their name: the last Song emperor, fleeing as a boy, was given tea on the mountain by a phoenix.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Phoenix Dancong kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Phoenix Dancong style kit
revisions.text: Ya Shi Xiang, duck dung aroma, is the market name for a very floral Dancong, and most lists of the ten leave it out even though it sells widely. It is also called Yinhua Xiang, silver flower or honeysuckle aroma, a name put forward in 2014 for a scent likened to the wild honeysuckle of the mountain; many sellers keep the old name. Its line is traced to Pingkengtou village. Three stories explain the name, all told as stories: that it was chosen to put thieves off the bush, that it comes from the yellow local soil called duck dung soil, and that duck droppings lay on the bush. The tea tastes nothing like its name: every account of the cup gives flowers, usually with milk or cream, honey or fruit.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Phoenix Dancong kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Dark tea in general
revisions.text: Dark tea is made to be kept, and the trade values it more with age. Over years it turns darker and redder in the cup and grows mellower and sweeter. How fast it changes depends on how it is stored, and the trade does not agree on one way: some keep it cool and dry for a slow, clean change, others warmer and more humid for a faster, deeper one. When a tea counts as young or aged differs from style to style, so each style sets its own measure.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Liu Bao kit on its approval page, 2026-11-24

revisions.scope: Dark tea in general
revisions.text: Dark tea takes boiling water. Its leaf is mature and dense, so it gives up its flavour slowly and is hard to overbrew. Rinse it first with boiling water and pour that off within seconds: the rinse wakes the leaf and washes off dust and any stale smell from storage, and an old tea may take a second rinse. In a small pot use plenty of leaf, about 7 grams to 120 ml, then steep very briefly at first and a little longer each time; a good dark tea gives many cups.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Liu Bao kit on its approval page, 2026-11-24

revisions.scope: Dark tea in general
revisions.text: From a brick, cake or basket, ease the leaf off along the edge or from the top with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole pieces give up their flavour steadily; crumbs release it all at once and cloud the cup.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Liu Bao kit on its approval page, 2026-11-24

revisions.scope: Dark tea in general
revisions.text: Older or coarse dark tea is often simmered rather than steeped: the leaf goes into a pot of water, comes to a gentle boil and simmers for a few minutes. Thick leaf and long-aged tea release their flavour slowly, and the steady heat gives a fuller, smoother cup than short steeps do.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Liu Bao kit on its approval page, 2026-11-24

revisions.scope: Dark tea in general
revisions.text: A smooth, mellow cup with low bitterness and a deep red colour, often sweet and woody or earthy, sometimes with herbal or medicinal notes. A young dark tea can still smell of the pile or of storage; an aged one is usually redder, sweeter and thicker.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Liu Bao kit on its approval page, 2026-11-24

revisions.scope: Dark tea in general
revisions.text: Dark tea is Chinese tea whose leaf, after it is heated and rolled, is left to change in warmth and moisture, where microbes and the leaf’s own chemistry slowly darken and mellow it. Because that change comes after the leaf is made, the trade calls it post-fermented. In Chinese it is hei cha, “black tea”, which is not the English black tea; that tea is red tea, hong cha, in Chinese.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Liu Bao kit on its approval page, 2026-11-24

revisions.scope: Dark tea in general
revisions.text: The first records of dark tea by name are from the Ming dynasty, in Hunan around Anhua and in Sichuan, and in the late Ming it became a state-managed tea sent to the north-west in exchange for horses. In the Qing dynasty merchants carried the craft to more regions and more shapes, and some styles were made for new markets: Guangxi’s Liu Bao, for one, went to the tin mines of Southeast Asia. In the twentieth century state factories took over much of the making and settled the brick shapes that are sold today.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Liu Bao kit on its approval page, 2026-11-24

revisions.scope: Dark tea in general
revisions.text: Most dark tea shares four steps, each with a reason. The leaf is heated first, the kill-green, to stop its own enzymes from browning it; coarse leaf is often sprinkled with a little water so it heats evenly. It is rolled gently, because the large, mature leaf used for dark tea is tough and breaks if it is worked hard. It is then piled, and in the pile warmth, moisture and microbes do the darkening and mellowing, so the heap is turned to keep its heat in range. Finally it is dried, which stops the change and makes the tea stable enough to keep. Many styles then steam the leaf and press it, or pack it into baskets, and let it age.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Liu Bao kit on its approval page, 2026-11-24

revisions.scope: Dark tea in general
revisions.text: Dark tea was made for people who lived far from where tea grows: Tibet, Mongolia, China’s north-west and, later, Central Asia and Russia. The trade called it border tea. The tea had to survive months on the road, so it was pressed into bricks, cakes and logs, or packed tight in baskets. A dense, even shape is easier to carry, stack and strap to a pack animal, and it keeps better than loose leaf. Some dark tea is still sold loose.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Liu Bao kit on its approval page, 2026-11-24

revisions.scope: All red tea; Dian Hong where the origin is Yunnan
revisions.text: Dian Hong changes in storage, but the trade treats it as best in its first one to three years. It is kept for freshness rather than for age.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian in chat on 2026-11-24 (Approve all 15)

revisions.scope: All red tea; Dian Hong where the origin is Yunnan
revisions.text: Dian Hong takes hot water, roughly 90 to 100°C. A common start is about 5 grams to 100 ml, with short steeps that lengthen slowly as the leaf opens.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian in chat on 2026-11-24 (Approve all 15)

revisions.scope: All red tea; Dian Hong where the origin is Yunnan
revisions.text: A full, sweet cup, often described as malty, with chocolate or cocoa and honey notes and sometimes something floral. The liquor runs golden to bright red, and a good grade has little bitterness.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian in chat on 2026-11-24 (Approve all 15)

revisions.scope: All red tea; Dian Hong where the origin is Yunnan
revisions.text: Dian Hong is red tea from Yunnan, made from the province’s large-leaf tea trees. Its home is Fengqing County in Lincang, in the south-west of the province, and it is also made in other parts of Lincang and in Menghai, Pu’er, Baoshan and Dehong. Golden buds through the dry leaf are the mark of the style.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian in chat on 2026-11-24 (Approve all 15)

revisions.scope: All red tea; Dian Hong where the origin is Yunnan
revisions.text: When the war cut China off from its eastern tea regions, the country needed a new red tea to sell abroad, and the national tea company looked to Yunnan’s large leaf. Feng Shaoqiu reached Shunning, now Fengqing, in late 1938 and made a trial batch from one bud and two leaves. An experimental factory followed there in 1939, the start of today’s Fengqing factory. For decades nearly all Dian Hong went abroad; it was sold widely at home only from the 1980s.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian in chat on 2026-11-24 (Approve all 15)

revisions.scope: All red tea; Dian Hong where the origin is Yunnan
revisions.text: Yunnan’s large-leaf trees give a plump leaf with many buds, and a strong cup. The trade ties that strength to the leaf’s high polyphenol content, which is also why Dian Hong stands up to milk. The buds turn golden as the tea is made, so a tea heavy in buds shows more gold.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian in chat on 2026-11-24 (Approve all 15)

revisions.scope: All red tea; Dian Hong where the origin is Yunnan
revisions.text: Dian Hong follows the steps of every red tea: the leaf is withered, then rolled to break its cells so oxidation can begin, then left to oxidise until it turns from green to reddish brown, and then dried with heat, which fixes it and keeps the leaf golden. It is then sorted into grades. There are two broad kinds: gongfu, whole or strip leaf, and broken. The gongfu grades use one bud with one to three leaves, and teas of buds alone, sold as golden bud or golden needle, sit at the top. A grade name says nothing about where the leaf grew or how old the trees were.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian in chat on 2026-11-24 (Approve all 15)

revisions.scope: All red tea; Dian Hong where the origin is Yunnan
revisions.text: Two newer branches sell under the Yunnan red name. Old-tree red is made from old tea trees; it is priced higher, and there is no agreed definition or standard for it. Sun-dried red is red tea whose last drying is done in the strong spring sun of the mountains rather than over heat, a choice of process and not a separate kind of tea. The trade does not agree whether either should be called Dian Hong.
revisions.reason: Approved by Adrian in chat on 2026-11-24 (Approve all 15)

terms.pinyin: yī nián chá, sān nián yào, qī nián bǎo
terms.gloss: one year tea, three years medicine, seven years treasure

revisions.scope: Fujian white style kit
revisions.text: The trade says white tea is tea in its first year, medicine at three years and a treasure at seven; it is a saying, not a tested claim, and no agreed number of years makes a tea aged. With age it moves from fresh and sweet toward jujube, dried fruit, honey, wood and herbs, with a deeper, redder liquor and a rounder body. Keep it dry, clean and aired, away from strong smells and sunlight.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Fujian white kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Fujian white style kit
revisions.text: Gongfu style, use about 1 gram of leaf to 15 to 25 ml of water, for example 5 grams in a 100 to 110 ml gaiwan; weigh it, since the leaf is light and bulky. Silver Needle and young, delicate tea take water below the boil, about 75 to 90°C; older, leafier or aged tea takes water at or near the boil. Start with a steep of 10 to 45 seconds and add a few seconds each round. An aged cake is often rinsed quickly first, and older pressed tea can be simmered on the stove, about 5 grams to 500 ml for 3 to 10 minutes; young, delicate tea is not.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Fujian white kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Fujian white style kit
revisions.text: Pressed white tea is new. Cakes began in the 2000s and spread around 2010, because a cake is smaller and easier to keep and carry than loose leaf. A cake is made from one of several grades, White Peony, Gong Mei or Shou Mei, so its grade has to be read from its own description. Some cakes are pressed from leaf already aged loose for a few years, so the year on a cake can be the year it was pressed rather than picked.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Fujian white kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Fujian white style kit
revisions.text: In young Fuding tea: a sweet cup, floral, fresh and brisk, with the scent of the down. Zhenghe tea is most often called thick and full.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Fujian white kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Fujian white style kit
revisions.text: Fuding grows two named cultivars, Fuding Da Bai and Fuding Da Hao, and Fuding Silver Needle is made from their buds; Fuding Da Bai comes from Bailiu village in Diantou and has plump buds heavy with white down. Zhenghe has its own, Zhenghe Da Bai, used for its Silver Needle and White Peony. Both replaced, mostly from the late 1800s on, the older small-leaf local plants grown from seed, called Cai Cha.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Fujian white kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Fujian white style kit
revisions.text: Fujian is the home of white tea. Fuding and Zhenghe are its two leading counties, and Jianyang and Songxi make white tea too. Fuding is a coastal city in the north-east of the province, by the Zhejiang border, hilly over most of its land; its white tea is tied to Taimu Mountain, where the first mother tree and the first famous bud tea are placed. Fuding white tea is a protected origin name in China. Zhenghe is an inland mountain county further west.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Fujian white kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Fujian white style kit
revisions.text: Fuding buds are plumper and downier than Zhenghe's. In the cup, Fuding is most often called the lighter, fresher, more floral style, and Zhenghe the fuller, thicker, mellower one. That is the trade's comparison of the two places, not a rule for every tea.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Fujian white kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Fujian white style kit
revisions.text: The trade sorts Fujian white tea by how the leaf was picked. Silver Needle is buds alone. White Peony is a bud with one or two young leaves. Gong Mei has more leaf than bud, and Shou Mei is the mature-leaf grade, with large leaves and few or no buds, often from later picks. Fuding also makes a separate new-craft white tea, xin gongyi, which is lightly rolled after withering and is darker in the cup.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Fujian white kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Fujian white style kit
revisions.text: White tea in its present form is a Qing dynasty tea of the 1700s and 1800s, first from Fuding or Jianyang and from Zhenghe later in the 1800s. Fuding Silver Needle was first sold abroad around 1890. The stories of Taimu and older uses of the name white tea are legend, kept apart from this record.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Fujian white kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Fujian white style kit
revisions.text: Two steps make it: withering, then drying at low heat, with no fixing and no rolling for the classic grades. The leaf is withered in the sun, indoors in moving air, indoors with gentle warmth, or by a mix of these, as the weather and the leaf allow, usually for two to three days. It is then dried at low heat, over charcoal or by machine, until it keeps.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Fujian white kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Fujian white style kit
revisions.text: Jujube or dried dates, herbs and medicine, wood, honey and dried fruit, a deeper, redder liquor, a thicker, rounder body, and less lift in the scent than a young tea.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the Fujian white kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: GABA oolong process kit
revisions.text: In a cup or pot, steep it for about two to five minutes. It is forgiving of small changes in water temperature and steeping time. It can also be cold-brewed, steeped for some hours in the fridge.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the GABA oolong kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: GABA oolong process kit
revisions.text: Ripe, dried or stewed fruit such as apricot, honeyed sweetness, a smooth, round body, and little bitterness or astringency; often brown sugar or roasted grain, sometimes wood or spice, and a light fruity sourness.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the GABA oolong kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: GABA oolong process kit
revisions.text: GABA tea names a way of making tea, not a plant or a place. GABA, gamma-aminobutyric acid, is an amino acid found in tea leaf, and the leaf is treated so that the finished tea holds much more of it than ordinary tea. It can be made as green, oolong or red tea; oolong is the form Taiwan is best known for, where the tea research station named its version GABA oolong. In Japan, where the method began, it was called Gabaron, and in Taiwan the trade name is Jiayelong.

revisions.scope: GABA oolong process kit
revisions.text: The method was found in Japan, by Dr Tsushida and colleagues at the government tea research institute, and the finding is dated to 1987. The first Japanese teas had a stuffy, sour smell and taste, and Taiwan's tea research station changed the method and adapted it to oolong. It spread among Taiwanese makers, and Taiwan is now a main source of GABA tea sold abroad. It needs no special leaf: ordinary oolong types serve.

revisions.scope: GABA oolong process kit
revisions.text: The fresh leaf is held for some hours without oxygen, in a sealed chamber or drum filled with nitrogen or emptied to a vacuum. Without oxygen the leaf turns its glutamic acid into GABA and cannot break it down again, so it builds up. The leaf is then made in the usual way for its type; for oolong that means withering and tossing, fixing, rolling, drying and sometimes a roast. Taiwan's oolong method alternates rounds without oxygen and rounds in air, rather than one long hold.

revisions.text: Green tea is a tea to drink fresh. The sources read give its best time as within about a year of picking, and a shelf life of a year or two when it is sealed. revisions.scope: Green tea family kit
revisions.text: Green tea takes water well below the boil, about 80°C, a little cooler for the youngest leaf and a little warmer for older, larger leaf. revisions.scope: Green tea family kit
revisions.text: Green tea is the tea whose leaf is never allowed to oxidise. Soon after picking, the leaf is heated, and the heat stops the leaf’s own enzymes before they can turn it brown, so it keeps its green colour and its fresh, leafy taste. That sets it apart from red tea, where the change is let run to the end, and from oolong, where it is stopped halfway. Green tea is made in many provinces of China, Zhejiang, Jiangsu and Anhui among them, and in Japan, Taiwan and elsewhere.
revisions.reason: Adrian approved the green tea kit 2026-11-25

revisions.scope: Green tea family kit
revisions.text: Green tea is made in three steps, and each has a reason. First the leaf is fixed, heated fast in a hot pan or drum, or with steam, to stop the enzymes; the Chinese trade calls this killing the green, and it is the step that makes the tea green. Then the leaf is rolled, twisted and pressed, so it takes its shape and lets out a little juice. Last it is dried, by pan, oven heat or sun, until only a few percent of water is left, so it keeps and does not go mouldy.

revisions.scope: Green tea family kit
revisions.text: Green tea is sorted by how it is fixed and how it is dried. Pan-fired tea is dried in the pan and is the usual Chinese way; West Lake Longjing from Zhejiang, flat and straight, is the best-known example, and Biluochun from Jiangsu is curled into small snails. Steamed tea is fixed with steam, which is the usual Japanese way, and it gives a deeper green leaf and a grassier, sometimes seaweed-like taste. Oven-dried tea is dried over gentle heat after fixing, which leaves the leaf looser and keeps more of its white down. Sun-dried tea is dried in sunlight.

revisions.scope: Lapsang and Wuyi red style kit
revisions.text: Lapsang has no recognised tradition of long ageing, and no category of decades-old red tea is described. Over its first few years in good storage the pine smoke softens and moves toward dried fruit, wood and sweetness. Keep it sealed, dry, cool and away from light and other smells; a smoky tea scents whatever is near it.

revisions.scope: Lapsang and Wuyi red style kit
revisions.text: Zhengshan Xiaozhong is the red tea of Tongmu, in the Wuyi mountains of northern Fujian; its home villages and gardens lie inside the Wuyi mountains nature reserve. Zhengshan, true mountain, names the Tongmu core, and waishan, outer mountain, is tea made the same way outside it; how much that line says about quality is argued over. Lapsang Souchong is the Western name for it, taken from the Fuzhou dialect. In English the name now usually means the strongly smoked tea sold abroad, while in China Zhengshan Xiaozhong covers gentler and unsmoked tea too.

revisions.scope: Lapsang and Wuyi red style kit
revisions.text: Zhengshan Xiaozhong is called the oldest red tea, the ancestor of red tea, born in Tongmu; the dates given for it differ. The usual story is of soldiers camped among the picked leaf in the harvest season: the leaf spoiled, the villagers dried it over pine fire, and the smoky tea was sold to Dutch buyers. The story is told, not recorded. The tea reached Europe first through Dutch and then British trade, under names such as Bohea and Souchong. In 2005 Tongmu makers devised Jin Jun Mei, a red tea of buds alone made the Lapsang way but not smoked, and it changed the village’s trade.

revisions.scope: Lapsang and Wuyi red style kit
revisions.text: The leaf is withered, rolled and left to oxidise in covered baskets or cloth bags for some hours, until it turns reddish-brown to copper. It then goes into a hot pan, guo hong guo, which stops the oxidation fast, lifts the aroma and gives a sweeter, rounder cup, and is rolled again while hot, which shapes the strip and helps it take up smoke. In the traditional way the leaf is withered with pine heat in the qinglou and dried over the pine fire for most of a day.

revisions.scope: Lapsang and Wuyi red style kit

revisions.scope: Lapsang and Wuyi red style kit
revisions.text: The traditional tea is dried over a fire of local pine, and the pine smoke gives it its main aroma, with longan fruit said to sit in the same note. The work is done in a qinglou, a wooden house of several floors with the fire at the bottom and the leaf on bamboo mats above, so the heat and smoke rise through the leaf. The strongly smoked style was made for export and never took hold in China. An unsmoked Tongmu red tea now sits beside it, built up from about 2005 and made widely for the Chinese market. Cheap Lapsang from outside Tongmu is often flavoured or smoked by a shortcut rather than made in a qinglou.

revisions.scope: Liu An basket tea style kit
revisions.text: The tea is packed into woven bamboo baskets lined with bamboo leaf, from about 250 to 600 grams each, several tied into a bundle. The leaf lining gives the tea a bamboo note that sellers liken to rice dumplings, and drinkers keep the leaves to brew a small piece with the tea. Old baskets carry printed paper tickets naming the firm, which collectors use to tell editions and fakes apart. Sun Yi Shun is the best-known old firm, but modern baskets carry the name too, so the name alone does not date a basket.

revisions.scope: Liu An basket tea style kit
revisions.text: Liu An basket tea is a dark tea packed into small bamboo baskets and kept for years. Despite its name it is made in Qimen County in southern Anhui, around Luxi and Rongkou, not in Lu'an, from the local small-leaf Qimen bush that Keemun red tea also comes from. In the south it was sold as Liu An, and sellers today use Liu An, Lu An, Lao Liu An and An tea for the same basket tea; the name is said to come from its following the Liu An way of making and trading. It is not Liu An Gua Pian, a green tea from the Lu'an area that only shares part of the name.

revisions.scope: Liu An basket tea style kit
revisions.text: Spring leaf, picked around Grain Rain, is first made much like a green tea: withered, fixed, rolled and dried into rough tea, which rests through the summer. In early autumn it is sorted, graded, blended and fired over charcoal. Then comes the step most accounts single out: the fired tea is spread on bamboo mats outdoors for one night to take the dew, and gathered before sunrise. It is steamed soft, packed into baskets lined with bamboo leaf, tied into bundles and fired a last time over charcoal, and it is sold only after resting for some years, commonly three.

revisions.scope: Liu Bao tea

It is dried slowly over a wood or pine fire, which can leave a faint smoke and keeps the leaf sound enough to age. Then it is packed tight into bamboo baskets and rested in a cool, damp, dark store for one to three years before it is sold.

revisions.scope: All oolong; Taiwan oolong where the origin is Taiwan, its four style sections only on teas named for them
revisions.text: Only well-made, well-roasted oolong is kept to age; the families most often aged are Wuyi rock tea, traditional Tieguanyin and roasted Taiwan oolong. Light, green-style oolong is a tea to drink fresh, and kept too long it goes flat or sour. Moisture is the danger: tea that was not dried and roasted enough takes up damp and turns grassy again. The heavier the roast, the more slowly the tea changes. Over years of storage good oolong is roasted again at low heat from time to time to drive off the moisture it has taken in, a skilled job that can cost some quality each round. Kept sealed, away from light, smells and damp, a roasted oolong softens with the years: the roast loses its edge, the body grows smoother and thicker, the liquor deepens towards red-brown, and the high floral aroma fades. There are no agreed ages at which oolong counts as aged.

A common start is about 4 to 6 grams to 100 ml, with a first steep of roughly 5 to 15 seconds and 5 to 10 seconds more each round. Light, green-style oolong takes water a little off the boil, about 90 to 95°C; heavily oxidised, roasted and aged oolong takes water at a full boil. Many people pour a quick first rinse to wake tightly rolled leaf. In a larger pot, use less leaf and steep for a few minutes.

revisions.text: Oolong is made in four main families, each named for where it comes from and how it is made, not for quality. North Fujian makes Wuyi rock tea, strip-rolled, usually the most oxidised and most roasted, prized for a lasting mineral quality the trade calls rock rhyme. South Fujian, led by Anxi and its Tieguanyin, makes ball-rolled tea. The Phoenix mountain area of Chaozhou in Guangdong makes Dan Cong, strip-rolled and mostly named for its aroma, which comes from the bush and not from added flavour. Taiwan, whose tea came from Fujian, makes mostly light to medium oolong, usually ball-rolled, with high mountain tea the most popular style.

The craft then spread to Chaozhou and to Taiwan, where oolong grew into an export tea in the second half of the nineteenth century. Where oolong first began, Wuyi or Anxi, is not settled, and the stories told about its name and its first makers are stories.

revisions.scope: All oolong; Taiwan oolong where the origin is Taiwan, its four style sections only on teas named for them
revisions.text: Oolong is made in a set order, and each step has a reason. The leaf is withered, often first in the sun and then indoors, so it goes soft enough to handle without breaking. It is then tossed or shaken in rounds with rests between them. The knocking bruises the leaf’s edges, which begin to oxidise, and the rests let the change spread slowly inward while the aroma builds. That is why a well-made oolong leaf is often green in the middle with a reddish edge. High heat, in a wok or a hot drum, then stops the change at the level the maker wants. The leaf is rolled, either into long twisted strips or, by rolling again and again in cloth, into tight balls. Last, it is dried, and many oolongs are then roasted.

revisions.scope: Trade history before 1973
revisions.text: Before 1949, pu’er already reached Hong Kong and Guangzhou red in the cup. Leaf was packed damp into bamboo baskets, the caravan journey could take a year, and merchants kept the tea for years more before selling it. When faster transport brought fresher tea in the 1950s, those drinkers missed the old taste, and the trade set out to hurry it. In Macau and Hong Kong, Lu Zhuxun sprinkled leaf with water to speed its change. From 1959 the Guangdong tea company in Guangzhou developed a faster fermentation, often blending Yunnan leaf with Guangdong leaf. Yunnan had its own beginnings too: dampening leaf for its pressed jin cha, and in 1958 a steam method at Xiaguan that cut fermentation to about fifteen days.

revisions.scope: The wet-pile process in general
revisions.text: Ripe pu’er is made by fermenting tea leaves in a damp pile, a process called wet piling. Sun-dried leaf is wetted and heaped so that heat, moisture and microbes can work on it. The heat comes from the microbes themselves, so the pile is covered to hold it in, then turned about once a week to spread it and let air in. It is kept below about 65°C, because hotter than that the leaf starts to char. After one to two months the leaf is dried. Yunnan’s state factories brought the method into production in 1973, after a joint team studied faster piling in Guangdong.

revisions.scope: Sichuan border tea style kit
revisions.text: Sichuan border tea is a dark tea made around Ya'an in western Sichuan and pressed into dense bricks for the Tibetan highlands. revisions.scope: Sichuan border tea style kit
revisions.text: The making has two stages. First comes rough tea. The mature leaf is heated to stop its own enzymes, then steamed, rolled and piled in repeated rounds, so that warmth, moisture and microbes darken and mellow it. Accounts count the steps differently, from about 18 to more than 30. Then comes the brick. The rough tea is sorted and blended for the style, steamed, pressed and dried, and rested in a pile so that it keeps changing around the pressing. Accounts differ on whether the rest comes before or after the press. The steam softens the coarse leaf so that it holds together as a brick, and the blend is how the maker sets how much leaf and how much red moss go in.

revisions.scope: Oolong from the Wuyi mountains; Da Hong Pao, Rougui, Shui Xian and Meizhan only on teas named for them
revisions.text: Wuyi tea follows the oolong steps: it is withered in the sun and then cooled indoors, shaken and rested, fixed in a hot pan or drum, rolled into strips and given a first drying. Much of it is now made with machines guided by hand judgement, and fully hand-made tea is rare. What sets it apart is the roast: over charcoal, in several rounds with rests of weeks or months between them, not in one pass. The roast dries the tea so it keeps, and it takes away the raw, grassy taste, deepens the tea and adds fruit and a charcoal fragrance. The roast is matched to the leaf: thick, mature leaf takes a stronger roast, thin and aromatic leaf a lighter one.

revisions.scope: jingmai
revisions.text: Jingmai is a tea mountain in Huimin Town, Lancang Lahu Autonomous County, in Pu’er City, Yunnan. Its old tea forests and villages were listed together as a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape in 2023. revisions.scope: jingmai

revisions.scope: kunlu-mountain
revisions.text: Kunlu Mountain is a spur of the Wuliang Mountains in Ning’er Hani and Yi Autonomous County, Pu’er City, Yunnan. The name is also written with other characters in older writing. revisions.scope: kunlu-mountain

revisions.scope: kunlu-mountain
revisions.text: In the Qing period, tea from Kunlu was made as tribute tea and carried to Beijing by horse caravan, about two months along the Tea Horse Road. Making Pu’er tribute tea in Ning’er is now listed as national intangible cultural heritage. Many sellers call the mountain an imperial tea garden, but the date and the details of that role are not settled.

revisions.scope: kunlu-mountain

revisions.scope: tea-heads
revisions.text: Tea heads are dense clumps of leaf that stick together while ripe pu’er is wet piled. They are sorted out after piling and sold on their own, loose or pressed, apart from the numbered grades of loose ripe tea.

revisions.scope: tea-heads
revisions.text: Pectin from the leaf, with heat and the weight of the pile, glues leaf into lumps, and microbes keep working inside them. After piling, workers pick the lumps out and try to loosen them. Lumps too tight to break without crushing the leaf are set aside as tea heads. They are about 0.8 to 1.5 percent of a batch.

revisions.scope: tea-heads

revisions.scope: Anhua County as a place: province, city, river, mountains, terrain
revisions.text: Anhua is a mountain county in north-central Hunan, in the city of Yiyang. It lies on the middle stretch of the Zi river, at the northern foot of the Xuefeng mountains, and is the southernmost and westernmost county of Yiyang. Most of the land is hills and steep valleys, with streams running down to the river. It is a place where rice is hard to grow and tea does well.

revisions.scope: Anhua County's climate, soil, forest and local large-leaf tea, and why the trade ties dark tea character to the place
revisions.text: People value Anhua first as the home of Chinese dark tea, and then for the ground the tea grows in. The county is warm and very wet, with four clear seasons, a short cold spell, and cloud and mist on the high mountains such as Yuntai. The slopes on both sides of the river are deep, loose, slightly acidic soil weathered from shale, which drains well. A large share of the county is forest, and the tea sits among it, not on cleared plains. The local large-leaf tea, best known from Yuntai Mountain, has thick, soft leaf that suits dark tea making. In Anhua the same wet, warm air that helps the tea grow is also the air the tea is piled, pressed and aged in, which is why the trade ties the character of the finished tea to the place and not only to the method.

revisions.scope: How Anhua became a county and a tea county, in outline; the tea's own history is on the Anhua dark tea page
revisions.text: Anhua was set up as a county in the Northern Song, after the Meishan hill country was opened to the outside world, and tea has been recorded in the area since the Tang. The trade grew under the Ming and Qing, when Anhua tea went north and north-west by road and river to the north-west and on to Russia. Old stone paths and merchant towns such as Tangjiaguan, a stop on the long tea road, still show where that trade passed. For the tea itself, how it was made and what it became, see the Anhua dark tea page.

revisions.scope: Tea as the main industry of Anhua County today, in general terms
revisions.text: Tea is the main industry of Anhua. Tea gardens cover a large part of the hills, more than two hundred firms process the leaf, and hundreds of thousands of people in and around the county make a living from tea in some way. Visitors come to the tea museum, the old tea roads and the tea farms on Yuntai Mountain, so the place is also a destination in its own right.

revisions.scope: Anxi County as a place: location and landscape
revisions.text: Anxi is a county in southern Fujian, in the prefecture of Quanzhou, inland from the coast and north of Xiamen. It sits on the southern side of the Daiyun mountains. The county town lies in a low basin, and the land rises into hills and ridges all round it. Anxi is the home of Tieguanyin and one of the main oolong counties of China.

revisions.scope: Anxi County: climate, soil and gardens, as the trade describes them in general; not any one garden
revisions.text: Anxi is warm, wet and misty, with mild winters and rain through most of the year. The mountains are weathered granite, which breaks down into acidic, free-draining red and yellow soil, the kind tea likes. Farmers build terraced gardens on the slopes, keep forest on the ridges above, and farm the foothills and river valleys below. The higher gardens have cooler nights, more fog and slower growth, and sellers connect that with a more concentrated, more fragrant leaf. The soil is not strongly mineral the way Wuyi rock is, so Anxi tea is usually described through its cultivar and its making more than through its ground.

revisions.scope: Anxi County: what it is known for as a whole; not a description of any single tea
revisions.text: Anxi is known for oolong, and above all for Tieguanyin, which fills most of the county's tea land. Anxi is also where the trade places the craft of oolong making in southern Fujian, and where farmers learned to grow new plants from cuttings and layers instead of seed. Alongside Tieguanyin, four other local cultivars are well known: Huangjingui (also called Huangdan), Benshan, Maoxie and Meizhan. Each is sold as its own tea, and none of them is Tieguanyin. For the tea itself, how it is made and how it is sorted, see the Tieguanyin page.

revisions.scope: Named Anxi townships and the styles trade writing links them with; a pointer, not a grade or a guarantee
revisions.text: Trade writing treats a few Anxi townships as names in their own right. Xiping, in the west, is where Tieguanyin is said to have begun, and its teas are usually described as the traditional kind, more oxidised and often roasted. Xianghua is high and often in cloud, and its tea is known for a strong, lasting taste. Gande is the newest of the three, lower, with younger bushes, and is tied to the lighter, greener style. Changkeng is often named as a fourth. Away from Tieguanyin, Daping is linked to Maoxie, Huqiu to Huangjingui and Lutian to Meizhan. A township is a pointer to the style of tea you may meet and is not a grade.

revisions.scope: The trade habit of splitting Anxi into inner and outer; the boundary is not fixed
revisions.text: Sellers often speak of inner Anxi, the high mountain areas, and outer Anxi, the lower, warmer land nearer the county town. Inner Anxi is said to give the deeper, longer-lasting tea, and outer Anxi a quicker, brighter fragrance but a thinner cup. Places draw the line between the two in different ways, so treat it as a rough guide to height and not as a fixed border.

revisions.scope: Anxi County: tea history in outline; Tieguanyin origin stories are folk accounts
revisions.text: Anxi has grown tea for many centuries, and local sources trace it back to the late Tang. Tieguanyin itself is told as a story of the 1700s in Xiping, and the stories are folk accounts and not records. Oolong from southern Fujian was shipped out through Quanzhou and later Xiamen, and families from Anxi, many of them from Xiping, carried the tea and the trade to Southeast Asia, where they opened tea houses. Tea is still the main income of the county. Until the 1990s Anxi was one of the poorer counties in Fujian, and the Tieguanyin boom that followed changed that.

revisions.scope: What Anxi means on a label; place only, not style or grade
revisions.text: Anxi Tieguanyin is a protected name, and Anxi on a label is a statement about where the leaf grew. It says nothing about the style, which can be light and green or roasted, and nothing about the grade. Not every tea sold as Tieguanyin comes from Anxi: some is grown elsewhere, and some is made from other cultivars under the name. A township on a label, such as Xiping or Xianghua, is a narrower claim than Anxi, and a label rarely proves it.

revisions.scope: State tea trading company founded 1949, parent of the Zhong Cha brand
revisions.text: China National Tea Corporation, known in pu’er circles as Zhong Cha, CNNP or China Tea, began in 1949 as the state’s national tea trading company, set up soon after the People’s Republic was founded. It organised tea production, export and sales across the country, and in Yunnan it stood above the big state factories. The name has changed with the state’s trade bodies over the years, and the sources do not agree on every step, so this page does not try to give one clean chain of names.

revisions.scope: The Zhong Cha trademark and its design, early 1950s
revisions.text: The Zhong Cha trademark is a green character for tea, cha, ringed by eight red characters for zhong, which is why the trade also calls it the “eight zhong” mark. It dates from the early 1950s. Sources give 1951 for the trademark and 1952 for the finished look of the logo, so the exact year is not settled. It is one of the oldest tea marks in China and is the sign most people mean when they say a pu’er is “Zhong Cha”.

revisions.scope: Which makers produced pu'er under the mark, and how that changed
revisions.text: Through the state era, pu’er from several Yunnan factories reached the market under the Zhong Cha mark, chiefly Kunming, Menghai and Xiaguan. The company was the trader and brand owner, and the factories made the tea. After the factories moved to their own brands in the 1980s and 1990s, Zhong Cha was also put on tea from smaller and newer makers. For that reason the mark belongs to the company, not to one factory or one style of tea.

revisions.scope: What a Zhong Cha label does and does not tell you about one tea
revisions.text: A Zhong Cha label says who sold the tea. It does not say which factory made it, which leaf went in, or how good it is, and teas under the mark vary a great deal from one era and one maker to the next. A factory’s history is not a fact about every tea under this name. What a given cake is, and what its own designation such as Red Seal or Blue Seal Green Label means, belongs on that tea’s own page, not here.

revisions.text: The company is now part of COFCO, the state grain and food group, and it still sells tea, pu’er among it, under the Zhong Cha name. That brief gap is reported by only a few places, so it is not stated as settled.

revisions.scope: Where Yiwu sits: Mengla County, east of the Lancang River, one of the Six Famous Tea Mountains; any tea whose origin says Yiwu.
revisions.text: Yiwu is in the north of Mengla County, the eastern county of Xishuangbanna in southern Yunnan, on the east side of the Lancang River (the upper Mekong). It is one of the old Six Famous Tea Mountains, and the town of Yiwu has long been where tea from the surrounding villages is gathered and processed. Mahei, Mansa and Luoshuidong are among the villages around it where old trees still grow.

revisions.scope: The regional tendency of Yiwu raw pu'er (soft, sweet, floral and honeyed, little bitterness); not a promise for any single tea.
revisions.text: Yiwu is known for raw pu’er that drinks soft and sweet rather than forceful. The trade describes a smooth, thick liquor with little bitterness, a floral and honeyed fragrance, and a sweet aftertaste that lasts through many infusions. People like it because it is easy to drink young and is said to hold up well with age. It is the usual contrast to the heavier teas of Menghai and Bulang. This is a regional tendency. The area is large, and the tea from one village can taste quite different from another.

revisions.scope: What the word Yiwu means on a label and how to read it; applies to any tea whose origin says Yiwu.
revisions.text: Yiwu on a label is a market name, and it is not proof of where the leaf grew. The word is used for the town, for the mountain and for a wider area, and sellers also use it for tea made with Yiwu leaf or in a Yiwu style. Some cakes sold under the name blend in leaf from elsewhere. The clearest labels name the village or plot as well as Yiwu, and a seller who can tie a tea to a village, a harvest and a maker is giving you something you can check.

revisions.scope: Guangxi as a province-level region and its two best known teas
revisions.text: Guangxi is a province-level region in the south of China, officially the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, and it borders Guangdong on its eastern side. Its tea is not one thing. Two very different teas carry its name: Liu Bao, an aged dark tea from the east, and jasmine tea from Hengzhou.
