revisions.scope: How Wuzhou city, Cangwu county and Liubao town nest inside Guangxi, as place names on Liu Bao
revisions.text: Wuzhou is the city in eastern Guangxi that anchors the Liu Bao trade, and Cangwu is a county under it. Liubao town, which gave the tea its name, lies in Cangwu. When a label says Wuzhou it names the wider tea area and the city's factories, and when it says Cangwu or Liubao it points to the original home of the tea. Making has since spread to other counties around Wuzhou, so the three names are nested rather than interchangeable.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Climate and setting of the Wuzhou area, as the trade links them to Liu Bao ageing; not the whole province
revisions.text: Wuzhou sits near the Tropic of Cancer, with a warm, wet, subtropical monsoon climate, plenty of rain, and hills and forest all around. People in the trade link this damp, steady warmth to the way Liu Bao ages slowly in cool storehouses, because the microbes that shape a dark tea like it. The soils are acidic, and the trade sees the setting as part of why Liu Bao is made here and not simply anywhere.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Guangxi's reputation for Liu Bao only; the style itself is on liu-bao
revisions.text: Guangxi is known above all for Liu Bao, a dark tea the trade values for how it ages. It matters to buyers as the one famous dark tea of the south, made for the hot, humid life of Chinese workers in Southeast Asia, and Wuzhou has grown it into a large industry with its own protected name. The style, its making and its aged stock are on the Liu Bao page, so this page does not repeat them.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Hengzhou jasmine scenting and flower growing; not Guangxi's other teas
revisions.text: The other tea Guangxi is known for is jasmine tea from Hengzhou, a county-level city. Hengzhou is described as the largest jasmine growing area in China, and a very large part of the country's jasmine flowers are picked there, which is why so much scented tea starts from its flowers. This is a scented tea of a different kind from Liu Bao, and the two share nothing but the province.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Reading Guangxi, Wuzhou, Cangwu and Liubao as place words on a label
revisions.text: Guangxi on a label names a region, not a style. A Guangxi dark tea is most often Liu Bao, but a tea from Guangxi can also be jasmine, and a tea made like Liu Bao elsewhere is not from Guangxi. The finer names, Wuzhou, Cangwu and Liubao, tell you more than the province does.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: Changtai, the company that owns the brand

revisions.scope: The Hengfengyuan brand name as used on Yunnan pu'er, and its place inside Changtai. Says nothing about any single tea.
revisions.text: Hengfengyuan is a pu’er brand name belonging to Changtai, a private Yunnan tea company based in Xishuangbanna. It is one of several brands Changtai sells under, alongside others such as Yichang Hao, which is the group’s better known Yiwu line. Little is published about Hengfengyuan beyond its place inside Changtai, so this page says only that.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Hengfengyuan as Changtai's ripe pu'er brand. Does not cover the maker or leaf source of any one tea.
revisions.text: Within Changtai, Hengfengyuan is the brand for fermented, or ripe, pu’er. The trade knows it for ripe cakes, tuo cha and loose ripe tea, and sellers who handle it describe the style as thick and mellow. A tea sold under the Hengfengyuan name is therefore normally a shou tea, which is how this one is sold.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: One line only: no place read links Golden Bull to Hengfengyuan; the link is the tea's title.
revisions.text: Golden Bull is covered on its own page. None of the places read for this page name Golden Bull together with Hengfengyuan, so the link between them rests on the title of the tea alone.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Which peoples are tied to Bulang, Nannuo and Mengsong within Menghai County; not every garden or village.
revisions.text: Menghai’s tea mountains are not one community. Bulang Mountain is the home of the Bulang people, and the Bulang are widely credited as some of the first to grow and make tea here. Nannuo is mostly tended by Hani families today (the Aini branch), although the Bulang are said to have planted its earliest trees. In Mengsong, most of the old gardens were planted by Lahu villagers. Who planted and who picks shapes each mountain’s gardens and its tea, so a mountain name is a better guide to a cup than the county name.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: How a Menghai label can mean the county or Menghai Tea Factory; says nothing about any one tea's leaf source.
revisions.text: Menghai on a label can mean the county where the leaf grew, or Menghai Tea Factory, which sits in the county and is part of the Dayi group. They are not the same claim. The factory buys and blends leaf from several Menghai mountains, and some of its ripe tea uses leaf from outside the county, such as Lincang. Its recipes and its history belong to its own cakes. A Menghai tea from a village or a small maker is not a factory tea, and a factory cake is not a single mountain unless it says so.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: How the old-tree gardens of Menghai County are generally kept, as against plantation bushes; not a statement about any single tea's garden.
revisions.text: What sets the old Menghai gardens apart is how they are kept. The trees are allowed to grow tall, with little pruning, and farmers use little or no fertiliser or spray. They give far less leaf than pruned plantation bushes, which are picked again and again through the season. People who buy old-garden Menghai tea are paying for that slow, low-yield leaf, and it is why the same mountain can taste so different from its plantation tea.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Nantou County as a place: landlocked, mountainous, central Taiwan; not any one tea.
revisions.text: Nantou is a county in the middle of Taiwan, and the only one that does not touch the sea. About four fifths of it is hills and mountains, rising to the Central Mountain Range in the east and to Yushan, the island's highest peak, in the south. Sun Moon Lake, the island's largest lake, lies in the middle. On a tea record, Nantou usually names the county as a whole, and a township or mountain inside it, such as Lugu or Shan Lin Xi, is the finer place.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Nantou County as Taiwan's largest tea county and why its range of altitudes gives different teas; not one style.
revisions.text: Nantou is Taiwan's biggest tea county, with more than half of the island's tea plantings and output. What makes it matter to a buyer is range. In one county the land climbs from low hills to cold mountain gardens, so it makes very different teas side by side: roasted oolong from the lower slopes, lightly oxidised high mountain oolong from the cool heights, and black tea near the lake. A tea sold as Nantou says which county it came from, and the township, mountain or garden says which of those teas it is.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: How the trade divides Nantou tea country by height; general, not exact ranges.
revisions.text: The trade splits Nantou's tea country by height. Low hills such as Mingjian grow tea for volume. The middle belt, around Zhushan, Sun Moon Lake and Dong Ding, is where roasted oolong is at home. Above about a thousand metres, around Shan Lin Xi and the high ground of Ren'ai Township, the gardens are cool and misty and make the light, sweet high mountain style. Which style a Nantou oolong follows depends on where in the county it grew, so the county name alone does not tell you whether it will be roasted or green and floral.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Where Lugu and Dong Ding sit within Nantou; does not define Dong Ding oolong itself.
revisions.text: Lugu Township, in the south west of Nantou, is where Dong Ding oolong comes from, and it is the best known tea place in the county. Lugu has grown tea for sale since the nineteenth century, and Dong Ding mountain is covered in gardens. For what Dong Ding oolong is and how it is made, see the Taiwan oolong page. What this page adds is its place: Lugu sits in the middle belt of Nantou, below the high mountain gardens, so it is a county of roasted teas as well as light ones.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Shan Lin Xi's county, township and character; altitude stated as disputed.
revisions.text: Shan Lin Xi is a high mountain tea area in Zhushan Township, in Nantou, and it is described as lying near Dong Ding. Its gardens are among the county's highest and are known for bamboo forest, mist and steep slopes. Places quote its altitude differently, from the low hundreds of metres up to about 1,950 metres in one account and 1,600 to 1,800 metres in another, so no single range is safe to state.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Ren'ai Township's high mountain tea, and that Lishan and Alishan are in other counties; Dayuling's county is disputed.
revisions.text: Ren'ai Township, in the east of Nantou, grows high mountain tea at roughly 1,100 to 2,000 metres. Lishan is next door but is not in Nantou. Sources place it in Taichung, and sellers sell it as its own name for tea grown above about 1,800 metres. Teas from the high ground between the two, such as Dayuling, are placed in different counties by different sources, so a seller's county for them is not safe to assume. Alishan, often named with these, is in Chiayi County.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Yuchi and Sun Moon Lake black tea as Nantou context; not oolong.
revisions.text: Yuchi Township, around Sun Moon Lake, is Nantou's black tea country. It grows Assam type tea, introduced in Japanese times, and its Sun Moon Lake black tea became better known after the 1999 earthquake, when growers there turned to it. It is not oolong, so it matters here only as the other half of Nantou's tea picture.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Where the Phoenix Mountain range lies and what a Phoenix Mountain label refers to.
revisions.text: Phoenix Mountain, Fenghuang Shan, is a mountain range in Fenghuang town, in Chao'an district of Chaozhou, in eastern Guangdong. It is the high ground of the Chaoshan region, with its top peak rising to about 1,500 metres. Tea grows on its slopes from low foothills up to roughly 1,100 metres, and the name on a tea label usually means this range as a whole rather than one village.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The climate of the tea gardens on Phoenix Mountain, and why the trade values it.
revisions.text: People value the mountain for the weather the tea grows in. Cloud and mist sit on the upper slopes for much of the year, the light is soft, and the nights are cool. The bushes grow slowly in these conditions, and the trade links that slow growth to the thick leaf and the lasting scent prized in this tea. The higher the garden, the cooler it is, and the more a tea is expected to show what the trade calls mountain rhyme.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Wudong and the named gardens of Phoenix Mountain; village character is not settled.
revisions.text: Wudong, the high ridge around the top of the range, is the part named most often as the heart of the mountain, and its high gardens are the ones the trade prices highest. Wudong village sits high on the ridge, with gardens near and above 900 metres. Da'an, lower on gentler slopes in Fengxi, is known for the largest old tea garden on the mountain. Other villages such as Shiguping, Lizipping and Guantou are also named, and each is said to give its own character, though little of that is written down plainly. A village name on a tea tells you more about where it grew than the mountain name does.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The old tea trees of Phoenix Mountain; no tree age is established.
revisions.text: The mountain is known for tea trees that stand where they have grown for hundreds of years, left unpruned so that they grow tall and send roots deep into the granite. A few are said to be 600 or 700 years old, and are tied by tradition to the Song dynasty, though no age is agreed or proven. Their leaf is made on its own and sold at very high prices, because each gives only a few kilograms a year. Most of what is sold today comes from bushes grown from these trees, not from the trees themselves.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The She people and Chaozhou gongfu tea in relation to the mountain; no start date for tea is established.
revisions.text: Phoenix Mountain is widely named as the homeland of the She people, who are tied to the tea of the mountain by local tradition. The mountain is also the home of Chaozhou gongfu tea, the small-cup way of brewing the region is known for. Tea has been made here for centuries, but no start date is agreed: sources give 700, 900 and more than 1,000 years.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The island's position, its central mountain range and why gardens sit on the west side; true of Taiwan as a whole
revisions.text: Taiwan is an island off the coast of Fujian, across the strait from mainland China, and its tea came from Fujian. A tall mountain range runs down the middle and the east, with many peaks above 2,000 metres, and the tea gardens are mostly on the western side. The range shelters that side from ocean storms, the climate is warm and wet, and the higher gardens sit in cloud and mist for much of the day.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: What Taiwan's tea trade is known for across the island; not any one tea or style
revisions.text: Taiwan is known above all for oolong. Its trade is built on rolled, bead-shaped oolong, much of it lightly oxidised, and on the high mountain teas grown above about 1,000 metres, where cool air, fog and short hours of direct sun slow the leaf and the tea tastes sweet and low in bitterness. Taiwan is also known for how many distinct styles it makes on one small island: roasted Dong Ding, the long-strip Baozhong, the heavily oxidised Oriental Beauty, and traditional Tieguanyin from Muzha. Black tea, green tea and newer oolong styles are made as well, but oolong is what the name Taiwan stands for.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Which counties and districts hold which tea areas, as the trade groups them; no area is described in depth
revisions.text: The tea areas fall into a few groups. In the north, around Taipei and New Taipei, are Pinglin, home of Baozhong, and Muzha, home of Tieguanyin. Further along the north and northwest, Hsinchu and Miaoli are where Oriental Beauty is made. In the centre, Nantou is the largest tea county, with Lugu (Dong Ding), Shanlinxi and the red tea around Yuchi, and it is joined by the Taichung mountains of Lishan and Dayuling. In the southwest, Chiayi holds the Alishan area. The east coast, in Hualien and Taitung, is smaller and makes a wider mix of teas. The high mountain tea areas are mostly in Nantou, Chiayi and Taichung, and the older, lower areas are mostly in the north.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: A short account of how tea reached and grew on Taiwan; no founding dates asserted
revisions.text: Tea came with settlers from Fujian, who brought plants and the craft of making oolong, and it grew into a trade for sale abroad in the nineteenth century, when oolong was sold overseas as Formosa Oolong. Under Japanese rule the island also turned to black tea, and in the late twentieth century more attention went to quality and to tea drunk at home, which is when high mountain oolong became so prized.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: What a bare origin of Taiwan does and does not tell a buyer
revisions.text: Taiwan on its own is a country, not a mountain, a county or a style. It tells you the tea was grown on the island and nothing more about where, at what height, from which cultivar or in which style. Two teas that both say Taiwan can be a roasted lowland oolong and a light high mountain oolong. Where a seller names a mountain or township, that is the fuller claim, and a bare Taiwan is the weaker one. The kind of tea, such as oolong, red tea or green tea, is a separate fact again.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: Wuyi Mountains; also the city of Wuyishan

revisions.scope: Location and protected status of the Wuyi Mountains as a tea place.
revisions.text: The Wuyi Mountains run along the border of northern Fujian and Jiangxi in south-east China. The tea town is Wuyishan City, in Fujian. The range is a UNESCO World Heritage site, listed in 1999, and much of it is protected forest and nature reserve. Tea grows in several different parts of it, from the river valleys to the high northern edge, and the parts make different teas.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The physical setting of Wuyi (rock, climate, fog) as the commonly given reason for its tea; not a claim about any single tea.
revisions.text: Wuyi is steep, wet and misty. The mountains hold in warm air from the sea, so rain is heavy and fog is common through the year. In the eastern part, red sandstone peaks rise out of the Nine-Bend River gorge as cliffs with flat tops. The west is mostly volcanic rock and granite. Tea bushes grow in the thin, stony soil of the ravines, on ledges and between rocks, where the ground drains fast and mist settles on the slopes. This is the reason people give for the mineral, stony character they look for in Wuyi tea, and for the slow growth of the bushes.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: half rock; the ring around the core
three pits and two streams; the best-known core sites

revisions.scope: The trade's zone naming for rock tea within Wuyi; describes a classification habit, not the quality of any one lot.
revisions.text: The trade sorts Wuyi tea by how stony the ground is and how close it is to the scenic core. Zheng yan, true rock, is the core of about 70 square kilometres, with steep rocky ground. Its best-known part is the three pits and two streams, among them Niulan Keng and Huiyuan Keng. Ban yan, half rock, is the ring around the core, with less rock in the soil. Zhou cha is tea from the flat, sandy ground along the river. Wai shan, outer mountain, is tea from farther away still. Most buyers and growers say the stony character fades with distance from the core, though the zones are a trade habit and not a guarantee of any one cup. The shop's page on Wuyi rock tea covers how these teas are made and judged.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: Tongmu village, source of Lapsang Souchong

revisions.scope: That Wuyi covers both rock oolong and Lapsang from the northern edge, from different ground.
revisions.text: Wuyi is known for two very different teas, and they come from different ground. Rock oolong, such as Da Hong Pao, Rougui and Shui Xian, comes from the rocky valleys and cliffs lower down. Lapsang Souchong, the original smoked black tea, comes from the high northern edge of the range around Tongmu village, close to the Jiangxi border, in forested country that is also protected. Tongmu is widely called the birthplace of Chinese black tea. Both are sold as Wuyi tea, so a Wuyi label does not tell you which kind you have. The pages on rock tea and Lapsang cover each.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: What the word Wuyi on a tea's origin does and does not tell a buyer.
revisions.text: Wuyi is a famous name, and it is used on a wide range of tea. The strict meaning of Wuyi rock tea is tea grown inside the Wuyi scenic area from the local cultivars and made by the Wuyi method. Tea from the outer mountain, the river banks or other parts of Fujian can still be sold with a Wuyi style name, and the name Da Hong Pao in particular is used loosely. A label that says only Wuyi or Wuyi Mountains, without naming a zone or a pit, does not say how close to the core the tea grew. Ask for the zone and the cultivar when you want to know.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Yuchi Township, Nantou: its location and its tea ground. Not any one tea.
revisions.text: Yuchi is a township in the middle of Nantou County, in central Taiwan, and it holds Sun Moon Lake. It is a basin of gentle hills around the lake, and its tea is grown mostly on slopes at roughly 600 to 800 metres. Tea from here is often sold under the name Sun Moon Lake, which is the better known name for the same ground.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The land and climate of Yuchi, as the trade compares them to Assam. Does not say any one tea tastes a certain way.
revisions.text: Taiwan is better known for oolong, so red tea in Yuchi needs a reason, and the reason is the land. The basin is warm and wet, with a lot of mist and cloud, deep reddish soil, and a lake that keeps the weather mild and steady. The trade, and the Japanese tea men who first trialled it, compared this to the Assam country of India, where red tea is made from the large leaf variety. That is why Yuchi became Taiwan's red tea place and not only a place that happens to make some.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The Assam planting at Yuchi. No year is stated. Does not cover other Taiwanese red tea regions.
revisions.text: Under Japanese rule, the colonial government wanted red tea for export and brought in large leaf Assam tea seeds from India. Trial plantings went in at several sites, and Yuchi was the one that did well. Sources give different years for the seeds and the first plantings, so no single date is safe to quote. The Assam type is the root of Yuchi red tea, and plantings of that type are still called Assam red tea here.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The Yuchi research station and the cultivars it released (Taicha 8, Taicha 18). Not a statement about every Yuchi tea.
revisions.text: A tea research station was set up at Yuchi to work on red tea, and the station still stands, now part of Taiwan's national tea research service (the Tea Research and Extension Station). Its work after the war gave Yuchi its named cultivars, among them the Assam type Taicha 8 and the later Taicha 18, called Ruby (Hong Yu), a cross of a Taiwanese wild tea with a Burmese large leaf red tea. The cultivar is a separate fact from the place: Yuchi makes red tea from more than one of them.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The township's red tea industry over time. Not a statement about prices or any one producer.
revisions.text: Red tea from Yuchi was an export crop and it faded when it could no longer compete. From the 1970s rising wages made hand picked leaf expensive against red tea from other countries, and many growers moved to oolong or to other crops. The 1999 earthquake hit the township hard, and rebuilding turned attention back to local red tea. Since then a younger generation has returned to grow and make it, and Yuchi is again the first place most people name for Taiwanese red tea.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: mark number; the trade word for a recipe code

revisions.scope: Where the Alishan tea area is and the range of heights quoted for its gardens; not a statement about any one garden
revisions.text: Alishan is a mountain range and tea area in Chiayi County, in the southwest of central Taiwan. It is one of the three best known high mountain tea areas on the island, with Lishan and Shanlinxi. Its gardens sit on the western and southern slopes, mostly at about 1,000 to 1,600 metres, though places quote the range differently, from about 700 up to 1,800 metres. On a tea record, Alishan names the mountain area. The county is Chiayi, and some records file Alishan under Nantou, which is not where it is.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: What the trade says about Alishan high mountain oolong as a style of place: climate, slow growth, light oxidation; general, not any one lot
revisions.text: Alishan matters to a buyer for its air and its approachability. Cloud and fog cover the gardens for much of the day, the sun is filtered, and nights are cool, so the leaf grows slowly and comes out thick and soft with little bitterness. The trade explains the cup this way: sweet, smooth and light in astringency, with a floral aroma that lasts through many infusions. Most Alishan tea is lightly oxidised, ball-rolled oolong with little or no roast. It is often the first high mountain oolong people try, and the style most buyers picture when they say high mountain tea.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The two cultivars most often grown in Alishan; says nothing about any single garden
revisions.text: Qingxin oolong is the main cultivar, and it is the one people most often mean by classic Alishan, with orchid-like or osmanthus-like fragrance and lasting sweetness. Jin Xuan, the milky cultivar also sold as TTES No. 12, is grown too, mostly on the lower and middle ground. Which cultivar a tea is, and how high it grew, changes the cup more than the name Alishan does.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The townships and sub-areas that make up the Alishan tea area; heights vary by garden
revisions.text: The tea area is wider than Alishan Township. Tea grows in three townships. Meishan, on the northern edge, has lower and middle gardens in villages such as Taiping, Ruili and Taixing. Zhuqi is the centre, with Shizhuo and Fenqihu. Alishan Township itself holds the higher gardens along the mountain road. Named sub-areas also carry weight with sellers: Shizhuo, Zhangshuhu and Ruifeng are among those most often named, and garden height varies a lot even within one village.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: How the name Alishan is used on labels and what a fuller claim looks like
revisions.text: Alishan on a label is a market name that covers a lot of ground, and it does not say which township, garden or height the tea came from. Tea from outside Taiwan, including high-altitude oolong from other countries, is sometimes sold as Alishan, so a bare name with no garden, height or cultivar is the weaker claim. Fenqihu is a related case: it is a tourist town with only a few tea gardens, and much tea sold under its name comes from nearby areas such as Shizhuo. A named village, a stated height and a cultivar make the fuller claim.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Where Anhui lies and which parts grow tea
revisions.text: Anhui is a province in eastern China, inland from the coast and crossed by the Yangtze. Tea is grown only in its south and west, in the hills and mountains: the Huangshan range and the country around it in the south, and the Dabie Mountains in the west. The flat north of the province grows none. Most Anhui tea sits in a few separate pockets, each with its own famous tea, so the name Anhui on a label says less than the name of the county or mountain does.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Climate and land of Anhui's tea hills in general; differences between south and west
revisions.text: The tea hills have a humid, subtropical climate with four clear seasons, plenty of rain, and mist and cloud that lie on the mountains for much of the year. People in the trade link that cover, together with acidic, well-drained mountain soil, to slow-growing leaf with a clean fragrance and a sweet aftertaste. The cold winters let the bushes rest, so spring leaf comes on strong. The west is cooler and drier than the south, which is why its tea grows on hardier bushes.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Anhui's best-known teas by type; not a ranking
revisions.text: Anhui is one of the great tea provinces of China, and it is best known for green tea. Three green teas carry most of its name: Huangshan Maofeng from the Huangshan area, Taiping Houkui from the Taiping area, and Lu'an Guapian from the Lu'an area in the west. Its one world-famous red tea is Keemun, from Qimen County. Several of these are on the lists of China's famous teas and the trade often names Anhui among the provinces with many famous teas. Besides these, Anhui makes smaller teas such as Huoshan Huangya, a rare yellow tea, and Liu An basket tea, a dark tea.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Four main tea areas of Anhui and the tea each gives
revisions.text: Four areas hold most of the fame. Huangshan, in the south, gives Huangshan Maofeng, a green tea with fine down on slightly curled leaf. Taiping, now part of the Huangshan area, gives Taiping Houkui, a long, flat green tea. Qimen, in the south-west, gives Keemun. Lu'an, in the west, gives Lu'an Guapian, a green tea made from single leaves with no bud and no stem, which is why it looks like a melon seed. Each of these is a separate tea with its own method, and none is a grade of another.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Keemun as the tea of Qimen County; its origin in the late nineteenth century
revisions.text: Keemun began in Qimen County in the late nineteenth century, when red tea making was brought into Anhui, which until then was known for green tea. It was sold abroad early and became a base for English blends. The trade describes it as a light, smooth red tea with a floral scent and little bitterness. Keemun in this sense is the tea of Qimen County and the hills around it, and the name does not cover other teas that are called Keemun style.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The difference between Lu'an Guapian and Liu An basket tea
revisions.text: The names Lu'an and Liu An look alike and are easy to mix up. Lu'an Guapian is a green tea from the city of Lu'an in western Anhui. Liu An basket tea is a dark tea made in Qimen County, in the south. It takes its name from the old Liu An way of making and trading, not from the city, and it is not green tea. A label that says Liu An or Lu'an needs the rest of the name to tell which tea is meant.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: Beipu, a Hakka township in Hsinchu County

revisions.scope: Beipu township as a place: location in Hsinchu County, low hill setting, Hakka character. Not a statement about any one tea.
revisions.text: Beipu is a township in the south-west of Hsinchu County, in north-western Taiwan. It sits in low hill country between the central mountains and the coastal plain, well below the altitudes of the high-mountain oolong areas. It is one of the most Hakka townships on the island, and the tea grown here is Hakka farmers' tea.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: bragging tea, a local name for Oriental Beauty

revisions.scope: Oriental Beauty as the tea Beipu is known for, and what that style is. Does not cover other Beipu tea or all Oriental Beauty from elsewhere.
revisions.text: Beipu is best known for Oriental Beauty, called Dongfang Meiren in Mandarin. It is a heavily oxidised oolong, close to black tea in how it is made, with a sweet, honeyed and fruity cup and little bitterness. Beipu is counted among the core places where it is made, together with Emei and Zhudong in the same county. The tea is sold under other names too, including Pengfeng tea and white-tip oolong.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Why Oriental Beauty from Beipu and nearby areas depends on leafhopper-bitten shoots, early summer picking and low spraying. Style-wide, not specific to one farm.
revisions.text: Oriental Beauty is made from young shoots that a small green leafhopper has bitten. The plant answers the bite by producing aroma compounds, and the leaf curls and takes on white, green, red and brown tones as it is made. This is why Beipu growers keep sprays off the gardens, and why the tea is picked only in the heat of early summer, when the insects are active. Because the leaf cannot be made to order, the harvest is small and the tea costs more than most oolong. Qingxin Dapang is the cultivar most often named as the best suited, with other cultivars also used.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: How Beipu relates to other Oriental Beauty areas and what a Beipu label does and does not say.
revisions.text: Beipu is one place among several that make Oriental Beauty. Emei and Zhudong in Hsinchu, the Toufen area in Miaoli and parts of Taoyuan and New Taipei all grow it. A label that says Beipu names a township. A label that says Oriental Beauty names a style, which is not limited to Beipu.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Where Cangwu County lies and its link to the town of Liubao
revisions.text: Cangwu is a county of Wuzhou city, in eastern Guangxi, close to the border with Guangdong. Its northern part is hill and mountain country, and that is where the tea is. The town of Liubao lies there, in the north of the county, and Liu Bao tea takes its name from the town. Cangwu is the original home of Liu Bao, the place the style comes from.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The mountain setting and climate of Liubao town in northern Cangwu
revisions.text: Liubao town sits among forested mountains, north of the Tropic of Cancer, in a warm, wet, subtropical monsoon climate. Mist and cloud are frequent, so the tea bushes grow in a good deal of shade, and the soils are acidic red earth. People in the trade point to this soft, damp, shaded setting as the reason the local leaf suits Liu Bao. It is the reason buyers who care about origin look to Cangwu first and to the rest of Wuzhou second.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: What Cangwu is known for: Liu Bao, its birthplace and its best-named villages
revisions.text: Cangwu is known for one tea, Liu Bao, and for being where it began. The town's own villages are the ones the trade names for prized leaf, and Heishi is the village most often mentioned beside Liubao itself. The county gazetteer of 1697 is the earliest record usually cited for the tea, and many accounts give the style a very long history, although that older date is not settled. What the style is, how it is made and how it ages are on the Liu Bao page, so this page does not repeat them.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The river route by which Liu Bao left Cangwu for Guangzhou, Hong Kong and Southeast Asia
revisions.text: Tea left the mountains by water. Merchants gathered it at the river landing of Hekou, below Liubao, and boats carried it down the Xijiang river through Wuzhou to Guangzhou, then on to Hong Kong, Macau and Southeast Asia. The trade calls this the tea boat road. It explains why Liu Bao was long drunk more in Malaysia and Singapore than in China, and why its history belongs to the overseas Chinese communities as much as to Guangxi.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The broad shape of Cangwu's tea industry from the war years to its revival after 2000
revisions.text: The river trade broke down in the war years, and demand from Southeast Asia fell again later. By the early 1990s very few tea gardens were still worked in the county, and some were cut down for other crops. Interest returned in the 2000s, helped by the wider rise of aged dark tea, and Liu Bao gained protected-origin status in 2011. Today Cangwu is one part of a larger industry centred on Wuzhou, not the whole of it.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The broad shape of Cangwu's tea industry from the war years to its revival after 2000
revisions.text: The river trade broke down in the war years, and demand from Southeast Asia fell again later. By the early 1990s very few tea gardens were still worked in the county, and some were cut down for other crops. Interest returned in the 2000s, helped by the wider rise of aged dark tea, and Liu Bao was registered as a protected origin in 2011. Today Cangwu is one part of a larger industry centred on Wuzhou, not the whole of it.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27); wording change only

revisions.scope: What the word Cangwu does and does not show about a tea's leaf on a label
revisions.text: Cangwu on a label names a county, and Liubao names a town inside it. They tell a buyer more than Wuzhou or Guangxi do, because the protected Liu Bao name covers the wider Wuzhou area and the leaf there does not all come from Cangwu. A label that says Cangwu is still not proof of leaf from the Liubao mountains, so a named village or a named maker backs it up better than the county word alone.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The name Da Xue Shan in Yunnan tea, across Lincang's four mountains of that name
revisions.text: Da Xue Shan means Big Snow Mountain, and Yunnan has more than one mountain called that. In Lincang alone, trade writing lists four: the Mengku one on the Bangma ridge in Shuangjiang County, the Bangdong one east of Lincang County, the Yongde one in the south-east of Yongde County, and the Fengqing one near Sanchahu. The name on a label does not settle which of them the leaf came from.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Which Da Xue Shan Chinese trade writing usually means (Mengku, Shuangjiang)
revisions.text: When pu'er writing says Da Xue Shan, it most often means the Mengku mountain: the main peak of the Bangma ridge, on the border of Shuangjiang and Gengma counties. Teas from it are often sold under the Mengku name. The Yongde mountain is the next most common, and sellers of its tea name Yongde or the reserve there. A seller who writes only Da Xue Shan has not said which one, and the other three are not rare enough to rule out.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The Mengku Da Xue Shan wild tea forest and its protection
revisions.text: People value Da Xue Shan for its wild tea trees. On the Mengku mountain a wild ancient tree community grows on the mid slopes in dense forest, at roughly 2,200 to 2,750 metres, and is described as large and well kept. The tea there is left to grow without pruning, fertilizer or managed picking paths. The core of that forest is now closed and protected, so it is no longer picked. Tea sold from the mountain comes from lower and managed ground.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Wild, ancient and plantation tea sold under the Da Xue Shan name
revisions.text: Wild tree tea, ancient garden tea and ordinary plantation tea are three different things, and Da Xue Shan is sold under all three. A cake described as wild arbor may come from trees tens of years old rather than from the ancient forest itself. Sellers describe raw tea from the mountain as strong and bitter, with a lasting sweet return, but taste varies by which mountain and which trees.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Reading Da Xue Shan on a label
revisions.text: Treat Da Xue Shan on a label as a lead, not a source. Ask which county the leaf came from, whether the trees are wild, ancient or planted, and what the seller means by wild. Menghai is sometimes named in this context, but a Da Xue Shan in Menghai is not established by the places read.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Dali Prefecture as a place in tea; Xiaguan's position.
revisions.text: Dali is a prefecture in western Yunnan, north of Lincang and well north of the pu’er mountains of Xishuangbanna. Its best known tea place is the town of Xiaguan, which sits between the Cang mountains and Erhai lake. Dali is a place in tea mostly because of what was pressed and traded there, and much less because of what grows there.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: bowl tea, a bowl shaped compressed tea
Xiaguan, the tea town of Dali

revisions.scope: Xiaguan as a compressed tea trading and pressing town; the tuocha tied to it. Not the factory's own history, which has its own page.
revisions.text: Xiaguan stood on the old caravan routes that carried Yunnan tea north to Sichuan and Tibet, and from the early twentieth century it was a gathering and pressing town for compressed tea. The bowl shaped tuocha is tied to Xiaguan: trading houses there are credited with developing it, and it is pressed there still. Sources give different years for when the shape first appeared, so no date is settled here. The trade at Xiaguan is the reason the name Dali shows up on pu’er at all.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: bowl tea, a bowl shaped compressed tea
Xiaguan, the tea town of Dali

revisions.scope: A Dali or Xiaguan name on pressed pu'er; not a statement about any one maker's blends.
revisions.text: Dali on a tuocha or cake says where the tea was pressed, not where the leaf grew. The Xiaguan trade has long blended leaf brought in from other parts of Yunnan, with Lincang counties such as Fengqing often named among them. Reading a Xiaguan tuocha as Dali leaf is a mistake. It is better read as a Dali pressing of Yunnan leaf, and the maker is a separate question from the place.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Tea grown within Dali Prefecture, mainly Cang mountains and Nanjian.
revisions.text: Dali makes only a small amount of tea itself. Gardens lie mainly on the Cang mountains and on the Wuliang range in Nanjian County, and what is sold locally is often green tea. Dali sits north of the zone where Yunnan’s large leaf tea trees are most concentrated, in a belt where large and smaller leaf plants grow side by side. Dali is not usually named as a source of prized pu’er leaf.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: Fuding, county-level city in north-east Fujian

revisions.scope: Where Fuding sits and its main landmark
revisions.text: Fuding is a county-level city in the north-east corner of Fujian, on the coast and against the Zhejiang border. Mountains close it in on three sides and the East China Sea lies to the east. It is hilly almost everywhere, and Taimu Mountain, a scenic and geopark area, is its best known peak.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: Fuding, county-level city in north-east Fujian

revisions.scope: The landscape and climate people cite as the reason for Fuding tea; general, not a rule for every tea
revisions.text: Fuding is where mountain and sea meet, and that is the reason most often given for its tea. Hills and mountains cover most of the land and forest covers well over half of it, so the gardens sit on terraced mid-slopes with forest above them. The climate is mild, humid and often misty, with sea air moving up the valleys, and the soil is acidic red and yellow earth. The trade ties this to the plump, downy buds that white tea needs, and to a tea that is usually described as fresh, sweet and floral. Many gardens are also grown with other plants and animals around the bushes, which the region now presents as a farming heritage in its own right.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: Fuding, county-level city in north-east Fujian

revisions.scope: Fuding's standing as the home of white tea and its main bushes; grades and styles are on the white tea pages
revisions.text: Fuding is known as the home of white tea. Fuding, Zhenghe and Jianyang are the three places in Fujian that make it, and Fuding is the one most often named as its origin. Its way of making white tea, a long natural wither without any frying or rolling, is listed as national cultural heritage in China. The leaf comes mostly from two local bushes, Fuding Da Bai and Fuding Da Hao, which together make up nearly all the tea grown there. What the types and grades of white tea are, and how Fuding and Zhenghe compare, is covered on the white tea pages.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: Fuding, county-level city in north-east Fujian
Bailin, a growing district in Fuding

revisions.scope: Named districts within Fuding; no agreed difference between them is claimed
revisions.text: Taimu Mountain and Bailin are the two places inside Fuding that the trade names most. Taimu is tied to the first famous bud tea and to the mother tree of the Fuding bush. Bailin is tied to an early bud tea of its own, known as white down tea. Diantou, Panxi and Guanyang are also named as main growing districts. Sellers say tea from higher and cooler ground is lighter and cleaner, and that each district differs in scent, body and sweetness, but too few places agree on how to tell them apart to treat any of that as settled. The year and the maker change the cup as much as the district does.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: Fuding, county-level city in north-east Fujian

revisions.scope: What the protected name Fuding white tea says about place, and what it does not
revisions.text: Fuding white tea is a protected origin name in China, recognised since 2009. On a label it means that the leaf grew and was made inside Fuding, which is a claim about place only. It does not say which grade the tea is, which year it was picked or how long it has aged. Taimu and Bailin are narrower names inside it, and a label rarely proves which of them is meant.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Fujian as a province, its capital and the four tea areas that have their own pages
revisions.text: Fujian is a coastal province in south-east China, facing Taiwan across the strait. Most of it is mountain and hill country, with short rivers running to the sea, and the provincial capital is Fuzhou. Tea grows in nearly every part of the province, and four areas stand out: the Wuyi Mountains in the north-west, Anxi in the south, Fuding on the north-east coast and Zhenghe in the north. Each has its own page.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Why Fujian makes many distinct styles: climate and separated mountain pockets, as sellers explain it
revisions.text: Fujian is warm and wet, with a subtropical monsoon climate, mist on the hills and mild winters. Its mountains and valleys cut the province into pockets with their own weather, and before modern roads the makers in each pocket worked on their own. Over centuries each area settled on its own plant varieties and its own way of making tea. That is the reason sellers give for Fujian making more distinct styles than any other Chinese province, and it is why Fujian on its own says little about what a tea is.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: red tea, the Chinese name for black tea

revisions.scope: The teas Fujian is best known for, as a list of separate teas and not a description of any one
revisions.text: Fujian is known for oolong, white tea and black tea, and it also makes green tea and scented tea. The best-known names are Wuyi rock oolong such as Da Hong Pao, Tieguanyin from Anxi, Fuding and Zhenghe white tea, Lapsang Souchong from Wuyi, and jasmine tea from Fuzhou. Smaller oolong traditions sit beside them, such as the pressed square cakes of Zhangping and Yongchun Fo Shou. These are different teas from different hands, so one of them is never a description of the whole province.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: A one-line contrast of Wuyi, Anxi, Fuding and Zhenghe; detail is on each area's page
revisions.text: The Wuyi Mountains make heavily roasted rock oolong and the original smoked black tea. Anxi makes lighter, floral oolong, above all Tieguanyin. Fuding and Zhenghe make most of Fujian's white tea, Fuding on the cooler, damp coast and Zhenghe inland and colder in winter, and the two are usually described as having slightly different tastes. The trade treats these as separate worlds of tea that happen to share a province, with different cultivars, craft and cup.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Fujian and Wuyi as the place black tea and oolong are traced to; dates are not claimed
revisions.text: Fujian is widely named as the birthplace of black tea, and Lapsang Souchong, from Tongmu village in the Wuyi Mountains, is the tea usually given as the first. Oolong is also traced to the Wuyi area, and its making is said to have spread from there to Anxi in southern Fujian, to Guangdong and then to Taiwan. How early either began is not settled, and the dates given vary from one account to the next. What the sources agree on is the place, with Wuyi at the centre. Tea shipped from this area to Europe in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries was sold as Bohea, a spelling of the local pronunciation of Wuyi.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The southern Fujian origin of the English word tea
revisions.text: The English word tea comes from the southern Fujian pronunciation of the Chinese word, close to te, which Dutch traders carried home from the coast around Xiamen. Languages that received tea by sea mostly say some form of tea, and those that received it overland say some form of cha. It is a small reason people link Fujian with the early overseas tea trade.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Reading Fujian on a label as a province name, not a style or an area
revisions.text: Fujian on a label is a province, not a style. It can sit on oolong, white, black, green or scented tea, and the teas differ in leaf, roast, oxidation and price. It also does not say which of the main areas the tea came from. For that, look for Wuyi, Anxi, Fuding or Zhenghe, and for the tea's own name. A white tea that names Fujian only may come from either of the two white tea counties, or from another county that makes it.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)
