revisions.scope: Guangdong as a province: position, climate, where tea is grown
revisions.text: Guangdong is a large province on the south coast of China, built around the Pearl River Delta. Its capital is Guangzhou, the old Canton, and Hong Kong and Macao sit beside it. The climate is hot and humid, with a rainy season and a drier one. Tea is grown mostly in the hills of the east and the north, away from the delta.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The two teas Guangdong is known for as a tea producer; not volume or the other teas made in the province
revisions.text: Guangdong does not grow tea on the scale of Yunnan, Fujian or Hunan, and the trade knows it for two teas rather than for volume. One is the oolong of Phoenix Mountain, called dancong, which is the tea most buyers mean when they say Guangdong. The other is Yingde black tea. Beyond these, the province matters for what happens to tea after it is made: where it is traded, stored and drunk.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Phoenix Mountain oolong as Guangdong's best known tea; details left to the phoenix-mountain page
revisions.text: The oolong of Phoenix Mountain, in Chaozhou in the east, is the province's best known tea. It is valued for its strong scent, floral or fruity depending on the bush, and for old trees that give each tea its own character. The mountain, its villages and its trees have their own page, so this page does not repeat them. On a label, Guangdong alone says very little, and the mountain or village name is what points to the tea.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Yingde black tea only; not Guangdong's other teas
revisions.text: Yingde, north of Guangzhou, makes the province's black tea. It is a young style by Chinese standards: machine production began in the late 1950s, and much of it has been sold abroad. Writers describe it as sweet, with a cocoa or chocolate note, and a malty, slightly peppery finish. It is not a mountain tea in the way Phoenix oolong is, and it should not be read as a fact about the province's other teas.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Guangzhou and Fangcun as a tea trading centre; not a statement about where tea is grown
revisions.text: Guangdong's weight in tea comes as much from its ports and markets as from its gardens. Guangzhou has been a gateway for tea leaving China, and its Fangcun market is described as the largest tea trading centre in the south, with thousands of shops and merchants from many provinces, Hong Kong and Taiwan. Pu'er in particular moves through Guangzhou, and for most of the last century its main buyers were in Hong Kong and Taiwan. A tea sold in Guangzhou is therefore not a tea grown in Guangdong.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Chaozhou gongfu tea and yum cha as drinking habits of the province; not a rule for every household
revisions.text: Tea is a daily habit here, in two very different forms. In the east, Chaozhou gongfu tea is the local way of brewing: small pots and cups, quick infusions, and a tea station at the front of many shops and homes. In Guangzhou and the delta, tea is drunk at yum cha, the morning or midday meal of a pot of tea with small dishes of dim sum. Pu'er, chrysanthemum and other teas are served this way, and pu'er has long been an everyday tea for ordinary people across the province.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Hong Kong and Guangzhou as named places of traditional pu'er storage; not a guarantee about any labelled tea
revisions.text: Hong Kong and Guangzhou are the places the trade names when it talks about traditionally stored pu'er. Both are hot and humid, which ages tea faster and darker than a dry climate does. Old pu'er sat for decades in the storerooms of Hong Kong teahouses and restaurants, and the "Hong Kong storage" label grew out of that. Whether a given tea sold under that name was really kept in Hong Kong, and how damp it was, is not something the label settles. See the pu'er pages for what storage does to the tea.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Hsinchu County as a place: north west Taiwan, hilly, mostly Hakka; not Hsinchu City.
revisions.text: Hsinchu is a county in the north west of Taiwan, with Taoyuan to the north, Miaoli to the south and the Taiwan Strait to the west. Most of it is hills and uplands, rising to the Xueshan and Dabajian ranges in the east. Most of its people are Hakka. Hsinchu City is a separate city and not part of the county, so on a tea record Hsinchu normally means the county, and a township such as Emei or Beipu is the finer place.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Hsinchu County as home of Oriental Beauty; not every tea made in the county.
revisions.text: Hsinchu is the home of Oriental Beauty, the honey-sweet, fruity oolong that is the county's best known tea. It is a hill country tea, grown on low to middling ground rather than on the cold high mountains of central Taiwan, and the style depends on the climate of these hills in summer, when a small insect feeds on the young shoots. A buyer who sees Hsinchu on a tea is most likely looking at Oriental Beauty, and the place matters because the tea is hard to make well anywhere else.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Which townships the trade names for Oriental Beauty; relative size of Emei and Beipu is from few places.
revisions.text: Within the county, Emei and Beipu are the two names the trade gives most often. They are neighbouring Hakka townships on the same river valley. Emei is described as the larger producer today, while Beipu has become better known as a heritage town with a historic old street and as a place to buy. Hengshan and Zhudong are also named as Oriental Beauty areas, and Guanxi is named in some accounts. Which township a tea comes from is worth reading on the label, because the county name covers all of them.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: lei cha; ground tea with nuts and grains

revisions.scope: Hakka character of Hsinchu tea making and Beipu lei cha; not a statement about any one tea.
revisions.text: Tea in Hsinchu is largely a Hakka trade. Local Hakka families grow the leaf, make the tea and sell it, and many farms have passed down through generations, with family tea making reaching back to the Japanese period. Hakka tea culture here also includes lei cha, a ground tea drink with nuts and grains, which is associated with Beipu. Farm visits and tea trails are now part of how the county presents its tea.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: How the leafhopper shapes Oriental Beauty as made in Hsinchu; does not describe other oolong.
revisions.text: Oriental Beauty depends on a small green leafhopper that feeds on the young shoots in summer. Its bite makes the plant produce the compounds that give the tea its honey and ripe fruit character, so growers avoid spraying pesticide on these gardens. The buds are picked by hand, usually the bud and the next two leaves, and the leaf is oxidised heavily, close to a black tea, before it is dried. This is why Oriental Beauty is a summer tea in Hsinchu, and why it is more costly to grow than an oolong that does not need the insect.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Names used for Oriental Beauty in Hsinchu; origin stories stated as unsettled.
revisions.text: Oriental Beauty is also called bai hao oolong, meaning white tip oolong, after the pale buds in the leaf. In Hsinchu it has an older folk name, pengfeng cha, which means braggart's tea. Stories about how it got the name Oriental Beauty, and about it being sent to a queen, are told in many places, but they differ in detail and are not settled history.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: What Hsinchu on a label does and does not tell a buyer.
revisions.text: Hsinchu on a label names the county, and it does not by itself say which township or what kind of tea. Oriental Beauty is not made only in Hsinchu, and accounts say that production has spread to nearby areas such as Miaoli and Taoyuan, so the county name is part of what a buyer is paying for. A county name with a township, such as Emei or Beipu, says more. Whether Hsinchu makes other teas in quantity, such as green or red tea, is not established here, though small amounts of Baozhong, high mountain oolong and black tea are served at local tea events.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: Hua Gang, a sub-area of Li Shan

revisions.scope: Li Shan as a tea area in central Taiwan and the altitude its gardens are quoted at
revisions.text: Li Shan, which means Pear Mountain, is a high mountain area in the middle of Taiwan, on the Central Cross-Island Highway. It is a tea area and also a town, with orchards of pears, peaches and apples around it. The tea gardens are the highest in Taiwan, at roughly 1,800 to 2,500 metres, though places quote the range differently and some start as low as about 1,450. On a tea record the name covers the whole area, and a garden or sub-area inside it, such as Hua Gang, is the finer place.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The high mountain oolong style and conditions of Li Shan, as sellers and growers describe it
revisions.text: Li Shan is valued for cold. At this height the nights are cool, mist and cloud sit on the slopes, there is little direct sun, and frost or snow can reach the gardens in winter. Leaves grow slowly, come out thick and soft, and are said to carry more sweetness and less bitterness. The usual tea is a lightly oxidised, ball-rolled high mountain oolong, most often from the Qing Xin cultivar. Sellers describe it as sweet, thick in the mouth and clean, with a fresh green finish. The cold also limits how often it can be picked: spring and autumn crops are usual, and the coldest gardens may give only two or three harvests a year or skip winter. That, with the cost of working steep ground at this height, is why it is priced high.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: How tea arrived in Li Shan after fruit orchards; no start date or planter established
revisions.text: Fruit came to Li Shan before tea. After the Central Cross-Island Highway opened, the high ground was settled and planted with temperate fruit, and Li Shan became known for its pears. Tea was planted among the orchards later, in the last decades of the twentieth century, and it spread because the leaf sold well. By the 1990s Li Shan counted as one of Taiwan's main high mountain tea names. Places do not agree on who planted the first tea or in which year, so no start date is given here.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Which county Li Shan belongs to and why records sometimes say Nantou
revisions.text: Most places put Li Shan in Heping District, Taichung City, not in Nantou. A few seller pages file it under Nantou, and it sits close to the Nantou border, near Ren'ai Township, which is probably why the two are mixed. A record that says Lishan, Nantou follows that looser habit. Treat Taichung as the usual answer for the place, and treat the county on a seller's label as a convenience.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: What the name Li Shan on a tea label does and does not establish
revisions.text: Li Shan on a label is a trade place name, and its edges are not fixed. Neighbouring high ground, such as Fu Shou Shan farm and the gardens near Da Yu Ling, is sometimes sold as Li Shan and sometimes under its own name. Some sellers say a tea sold as Li Shan should come from above 2,000 metres, but this is not a common rule. A label that says Li Shan but gives no garden, height or harvest season does not say much beyond the general area.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Lugu Township as a place: location in Nantou, setting, and what a record means by it
revisions.text: Lugu is a mountain township in the south west of Nantou County, in central Taiwan. It sits in the foothills of the Central Mountain Range and is a township of valleys, bamboo forest and tea gardens. Xitou, Shan Lin Xi and Dong Ding mountain are all known place names in or beside it. On a tea record, Lugu names a township, which is a finer place than the county Nantou and a larger one than any single mountain or garden inside it.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Why Lugu matters to tea buyers: its link to Dong Ding oolong, its mist and mountain setting, and bamboo; place only, not the tea's making
revisions.text: Lugu is known as the home of Dong Ding oolong, and for most buyers that is the whole reason the name matters. The place is cool and often under cloud and mist, with sunny mornings and foggy afternoons, and the trade ties the character of its tea to that weather and to the mountain setting. Tea shares the township with bamboo, and the bamboo shoots and bamboo goods of Lugu are as well known in Taiwan as its tea. This page covers the place only. For what Dong Ding oolong is and how it is made, see the Taiwan oolong page.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: Lin Fengchi, the man credited with bringing the bushes

revisions.scope: The locally told account of how Fujian tea bushes reached Lugu; dates and details vary by source
revisions.text: The story told locally is that tea bushes were brought to Lugu from the Wuyi Mountains in Fujian in the middle of the nineteenth century. In the most repeated version, a local man named Lin Fengchi returned from the mainland with a small number of seedlings, said to be 36, and some were planted on the slopes of Dong Ding. Places differ on the year, giving 1851 in some and 1855 in others, and on who planted what, so the details are told, not settled. What is agreed is that the bushes came from Fujian, that tea has been grown here since the nineteenth century, and that it grew into the township's main cash crop.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Dong Ding mountain and the higher Lugu gardens such as Dalunshan; altitude figures differ by source
revisions.text: Dong Ding is a mountain in Lugu, and gardens on and around it are where the tea took its name. Dong Ding mountain itself is not high, with one local source putting it at about 750 metres. Altitude for Dong Ding tea is quoted very differently, from about 600 metres up past 1,000, because the name covers more than the one mountain. Some growers have moved to higher ground in the township, such as Dalunshan, where gardens are described at about 1,250 to 1,500 metres. One account gives declining soil fertility on the old slopes as the reason. A tea from those gardens is still a Lugu tea, but it grows higher and cooler than Dong Ding mountain itself.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: What the word Lugu on a tea record does and does not establish
revisions.text: Lugu on a label or a record says the tea was grown in that township. It does not say the tea is Dong Ding oolong, and it does not say how the tea was made, whether roasted or not. Local grade marks that appear on Lugu tea are a separate matter from the place. The name Dong Ding is also used for the style when it is made outside Lugu, so Lugu is the stronger place claim of the two.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: Muzha, a hill district of southeast Taipei
Maokong, the tea hillside in Muzha

revisions.scope: Muzha as a place: southeast Taipei hill district, low hills, humid. Not a statement about any one farm.
revisions.text: Muzha is a hill district in the southeast of Taipei, in Wenshan District, on the edge of the city. The tea slopes are low hills of a few hundred metres, and Maokong, the best known tea hillside, is part of the same tea country. The area is wet, with a large gap between day and night temperatures. Growers and sellers say this resembles Anxi in Fujian, where Tieguanyin comes from.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: Zhang Naimiao, the tea master named for bringing Tieguanyin to Muzha
Anxi, Fujian, the home of Tieguanyin

revisions.scope: How Tieguanyin reached Muzha from Anxi, with the 1895 Zhang Naimiao account as the commonly named start. Later plant shipments are left out.
revisions.text: Tieguanyin reached Muzha from Anxi in Fujian in the late nineteenth century, carried by Fujian settlers. The trade most often names the tea master Zhang Naimiao, who brought plants over in 1895 and planted them in the Zhanghu part of Muzha. Many tea families in the hills still carry the Zhang name. Later shipments of plants are reported, but the years and numbers differ from place to place, so they are not settled here.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: Muzha Tieguanyin, the roasted oolong of Muzha

revisions.scope: Traditional Muzha Tieguanyin as a style: charcoal-roasted ball-rolled oolong. Describes the style, never the taste of a given lot.
revisions.text: Muzha is known for Tieguanyin made in the traditional Taiwanese way: a ball-rolled oolong, oxidised part way and then roasted over charcoal. It is far darker and heavier than the green, lightly finished Tieguanyin many people know from Fujian. The trade describes roasted and ripe-fruit notes, nuts and honey, an amber cup with a full body, and a sweet, lingering return. The slow roasting, repeated over many days, is a large part of why the tea costs more.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Muzha tea farms as visitor destinations. Background only, not a claim about any lot.
revisions.text: Tea here is also a place people go to. From the later twentieth century the city encouraged tea farms to open to visitors, and the hills now hold tea houses and farms that sell their own leaf. Most of those farms grow Tieguanyin. Buying at the source is common, which makes the farm and the year worth asking about.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: Tieguanyin from the true original cultivar

revisions.scope: What the words Muzha Tieguanyin do and do not prove about cultivar, place and roast.
revisions.text: Muzha Tieguanyin on a label names a place and a style of making. It is not proof of the plant. True Tieguanyin trees, often called zhengcong, give little leaf and need careful hands, and some growers in Muzha now use other cultivars such as Qingxin oolong for the same style of tea. Tieguanyin is also a name used for a way of making, so leaf sold as Tieguanyin may come from other plants. Place, cultivar and roast are three separate facts, and a label rarely gives all three. How the name sits with the wider tea is on the [Tieguanyin](tieguanyin) page.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Which northern Vietnam provinces and districts the old-tree tea comes from and the rough height of the gardens; not a statement about any one garden
revisions.text: The northern Vietnam highlands are the mountain provinces along and near the border with China, where old Shan Tuyet tea trees grow. Ha Giang and Lao Cai are the two most often named for this tea, and Yen Bai and Son La are usually listed with them. Within Ha Giang the trade names Hoang Su Phi and Vi Xuyen, within Lao Cai the Bac Ha area, and Suoi Giang is the best known grove on the Yen Bai side. Gardens sit high, mostly above about 1,000 metres, and the range is cool and misty.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: What Shan Tuyet means and how the trade describes its old trees and who tends them; ages are local estimates
revisions.text: Shan Tuyet means snow mountain, a name that comes from the fine white down on the buds. It names a family of large-leaf Shan tea trees and not one single cultivar. Many of the trees are old, with some said to be several hundred years, though ages are mostly local estimates and not measured. Mông and Dao communities look after many of the groves, and a number of old stands have been listed as Vietnam heritage trees. People value the tea for these old, lightly managed trees on forested slopes, in the same way they value old-tree leaf in Yunnan.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Why the trade compares the highlands with Yunnan; the history and size of cross-border trade is not covered
revisions.text: The highlands share the large-leaf tea trees, the mountain climate and the forest setting of the Yunnan hills just over the border. For that reason the trade often compares Shan Tuyet leaf with the leaf used for pu'er, and some sellers press it into cakes in the pu'er manner. How far back tea crossed the border, and how much of it is traded across it today, is not established here. The Vietnamese tea is its own product from its own country, and a comparison with Yunnan does not make it a Yunnan tea.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: How sellers describe ripe pu'er style tea made in the highlands, mainly Ha Giang; seller accounts, not a standard
revisions.text: Ripe, pu'er style tea is made here from old-tree leaf, mostly in Ha Giang, and some Lao Cai makers also list a pu'er style tea. Sellers describe a medium fermentation, which they say gives a softer cup than ripe tea from Yunnan, with woody, earthy and nutty notes and a sweet finish. Some keep it for several years in the humid mountain climate. The stated age and the trees behind a given cake are usually the seller's own account, so they are read as that and not as a standard.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: How to read a pu'er or Shan Tuyet name on a Vietnamese ripe cake; makes no legal claim about the name
revisions.text: Whether a ripe cake from Vietnam may be called pu'er is not agreed. Many people hold that the name belongs to tea grown in Yunnan, and some sellers of these teas say so themselves, calling the tea a Vietnamese dark tea made in the pu'er style. Others use the pu'er name freely. A label that says Ha Giang or Shan Tuyet gives a place and a tree type, and not a legal grade, a recipe or an age.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Where Qimen County is, in Anhui near Huangshan and the Jiangxi border
revisions.text: Qimen is a county in the south of Anhui Province, in the hills near the Huangshan mountains and close to the border with Jiangxi. It belongs to Huangshan City. Tea is grown in other parts of the same hill country, but the name Qimen on a tea record points to the county itself.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Why Qimen is known: Keemun, its setting and the Qimen aroma
revisions.text: Qimen is known for one tea, Keemun, the red tea named after the county. The land suits it: hilly, wooded ground with mild, damp weather, plenty of rain and frequent cloud and mist. Keemun is made mostly from a small-leaved local tea plant, and the trade prizes its scent above everything else. That scent is so closely tied to the county that it has its own name, Qimen aroma. People describe it as floral and fruity, sometimes with a faint smokiness, over a smooth, sweet cup with little astringency. It is one of the classic Chinese teas of the export trade, and it has long been used in English-style breakfast blends.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: Hu Yuanlong, usually named as Keemun's founder
Yu Gancheng, tea merchant sometimes given the credit
Rishun, name of the tea factory

revisions.scope: How Keemun began in Qimen in the late Qing, and the disputed founder
revisions.text: Before the 1870s Qimen made green tea. Red tea was made there from about 1875, using methods carried in from Fujian, by way of Jiangxi in most tellings, after green tea sales fell. Hu Yuanlong, a local man who set up the Rishun tea factory, is the name most often given as the founder. Another account gives the credit to the tea merchant Yu Gancheng, who opened buying stations in Qimen. The accounts disagree and the exact order of events is not established. What is agreed is the period, the late Qing dynasty, and that Western buyers were looking for the tea within a few years.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: What Keemun and Qimen mean on a tea label, county versus style
revisions.text: Keemun is a style as well as a place. Tea made by the Keemun method also comes from nearby counties in Anhui, such as Dongzhi, Shitai and Yi County, and from Fuliang in Jiangxi, so Keemun on a label does not by itself mean the leaf grew in Qimen County. The name also sells well, and tea sold as Keemun varies a lot in quality. Qimen, named as the place of origin, is the stronger claim. Black teas from Hubei sold as Hubei Keemun are not Keemun at all.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: three cranes; the Wuzhou Tea Factory trademark

revisions.scope: Three Cranes as the trademark of Wuzhou Tea Factory; says nothing about any single tea.
revisions.text: Three Cranes, also written San He, is the trademark of Wuzhou Tea Factory in Guangxi, the largest maker of Liu Bao. It is a brand of one factory. It is not a type of tea, a grade of leaf or a village, and other makers of Liu Bao do not use it. The story of the name, and of the factory behind it, is on the San He Liu Bao page.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: What a buyer can and cannot learn from the Three Cranes name on a Liu Bao label; the meaning of the numeric codes is not covered.
revisions.text: The mark tells a buyer who made the tea: Wuzhou Tea Factory, working in its own warehouses. Sellers also treat it as a sign of consistent factory making, which is a reputation and not a measure of any one tea. It does not say how old the tea is, which leaf it holds or how it is stored. Those come from the rest of the label: the harvest year and the year of packing, which are often printed as a pair, and a grade number such as third grade. The four or five digit codes that follow the brand name on many labels are recipe or batch numbers. What each digit stands for is not established here, so the number is best read as a lookup against the seller's own description.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Where the Wuliang range lies and which counties it crosses; a range, not a single village; peak height only roughly
revisions.text: Wuliang Mountain is a long mountain range in west-central Yunnan, not a single village or peak. It starts near Nanjian in Dali Prefecture, runs south through Jingdong, Zhenyuan and Jinggu in Pu’er City, and fades out toward Ning’er and the old tea mountains of Xishuangbanna. The Lancang River (the upper Mekong) lies on its west side, and the range runs beside the Ailao Mountains. Its highest peaks are a little over 3,000 metres, though places give different names and figures for the top.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Climate and forest of the range in general; not any one garden or county
revisions.text: The range has a monsoon climate: a warm, rainy summer and a drier, misty winter, with large swings between day and night. Climate changes a lot from the valley floors to the high ridges, so the tea on one part of the range can differ from another. Much of it is still forest, and part is a national nature reserve. Old tea trees sit in that forest and in small gardens near villages.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: That the range is known for old wild and planted trees, mainly around Jingdong and Zhenyuan; no tree counts or variety stated
revisions.text: Wuliang Mountain is known for old tea trees, both wild ones in the forest and older planted ones in village gardens. Jingdong and Zhenyuan are the counties most often named for them. Tree age, leaf variety and garden height are quoted differently from seller to seller, so none of them is settled for the range as a whole.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: What the name Wuliang means; the timing of its use on wrappers is stated as not established
revisions.text: Wuliang means “without measure.” The trade explains it as a name for a mountain too tall and wide to measure. When the name began to appear on tea wrappers is not established.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: What a Wuliang Mountain label does and does not tell the buyer, and how Kunlu and Qianjiazhai relate to the range
revisions.text: Wuliang Mountain on a label points to a whole range, and a label rarely says which county or village the leaf came from. Kunlu Mountain in Ning’er is a spur of the same range and has its own page. Qianjiazhai in Zhenyuan, home of a famous wild tea tree, is most often placed in the Ailao Mountains, not in Wuliang, though Zhenyuan sits between the two ranges and the line is not always drawn the same way. The trade says much tea sold as Wuliang comes from the northern part, near Jingdong and Nanjian.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: What sellers and writers most often note in the cup across the whole range; general, not any one lot
revisions.text: Sellers and tea writers most often describe a fragrant tea, with floral notes such as orchid, and a soft, fairly gentle cup with little bitterness. Some describe a fuller, sweeter body, and some find the tea thin. Reports differ because the range is so large and the teas come from different parts of it.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Wuzhou's position in Guangxi and on the rivers
revisions.text: Wuzhou is a city in the east of Guangxi, right on the border with Guangdong. It stands where the Xi and Gui rivers meet, and the stretch of river below the meeting is the road down to Guangzhou. The city has been a river town for more than two thousand years, and that position, not its own tea fields, is the reason it matters in tea.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Wuzhou as a river port and gateway to the coast
revisions.text: Wuzhou is the gate between Guangxi and the coast. Goods from the hills of eastern Guangxi came down the rivers to its port and went on by water to Guangzhou, Hong Kong and the sea. It was opened to foreign trade as a treaty port in 1897, and it is still described as the main river port of Guangxi. For tea this meant a simple thing: leaf made in the hills had to reach Wuzhou to reach the world.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Wuzhou's role in the Liu Bao trade, apart from any single factory
revisions.text: Liu Bao is named for the town of Liubao, which lies in Cangwu County under Wuzhou, so the tea is grown and first made in the countryside around the city and not in the city itself. Wuzhou was where it was gathered, finished and sent on. Tea came down from the hills by small boat and raft to the river, then by larger boat to Guangzhou, and from there by sea to the Chinese communities of Malaya and Southeast Asia. The trade still calls this the old tea-boat road. This is why Liu Bao is commonly called a Wuzhou tea even though Liubao town is the source of its name.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: Decline and revival of Liu Bao trade centred on Wuzhou, not exact output figures
revisions.text: Liu Bao sales were strong in the 1930s, then fell sharply after war reached the south in 1937 and the sea trade was cut. Later the planned economy and farmers leaving tea for other crops pushed output very low, and by the end of the 1980s very little was being made. Since the 1990s, and above all in the last fifteen years, Wuzhou has rebuilt the tea as a large local industry, with the city government backing it, new plantings, and a regional brand. Figures for output differ from one report to the next, so the size of the industry today is not settled here.

revisions.scope: What the word Wuzhou does and does not tell a buyer on a Liu Bao label
revisions.text: Wuzhou on a label names a city and its tea area, not a single maker. A Liu Bao sold as Wuzhou can come from a farm in Cangwu, from a factory in the city, or from one of the other counties around it, and the word alone does not say which. Liubao or Cangwu is the narrower claim and points to the original home of the tea. The Wuzhou Tea Factory is one maker in the city and has its own page, so its history is not the history of every Wuzhou tea.

terms.gloss: Three Cranes, the factory's Liu Bao brand

revisions.scope: The factory as one maker: opened 1953 in Wuzhou, state or cooperative owned, sells under San He (Three Cranes). Not a statement about all Liu Bao.
revisions.text: Wuzhou Tea Factory is a state-run Liu Bao factory in the city of Wuzhou, Guangxi, opened in 1953 as a tea works under the national tea company. It has stayed under state or cooperative ownership since, and was reorganised as a company in the 2020s. It is the best known single maker of Liu Bao, and it sells its tea under the San He brand, Three Cranes in English. Its own page covers the factory, not Liu Bao as a whole: farms in Cangwu and other makers in Wuzhou also make Liu Bao.

revisions.scope: The factory's export orientation and its place among the few Liu Bao makers around 2002 and the 2003 standard. Not a statement about farmhouse makers.
revisions.text: The factory grew up serving buyers abroad. For decades most of its Liu Bao went to Hong Kong, Macau and Southeast Asia, the places where the tea had been drunk since the mining era. As late as 2002 only two firms in Wuzhou made Liu Bao in any quantity, and this factory was one of them, mostly for export. When the first official Liu Bao standard was written in 2003, it was drawn from the practice of these makers, so the factory's way of working is part of how the tea is defined today.

revisions.scope: What the factory or San He name on a label does and does not tell a buyer.
revisions.text: A tea marked Wuzhou Tea Factory or San He names the maker. It does not name an age, a leaf source or a grade. It tells a buyer the tea was made in a factory, piled under control and aged in the maker's own warehouses, which is a different route from the farmhouse way. How a given cake or basket tastes still depends on its year and on where it was stored, so the maker is where reading a label starts, not where it ends.

revisions.scope: Xiaguan Tea Factory as a maker: its 1941 start in Dali for the Tibet trade and its tuocha. Not a statement about Dali's leaf or any single tea.
revisions.text: Xiaguan Tea Factory is one of Yunnan’s long-running pu’er makers, based in the town of Xiaguan in Dali, at the foot of the Cang mountains beside Erhai lake. It began in 1941 as the Kangzang Tea Factory, set up to press tea for Tibet and the border regions, and the trade still knows it for pressed tea above all. Its signature is the tuocha, a small bowl-shaped pressed tea. The shape is older than the factory, since Xiaguan tea houses were already pressing it decades earlier, and it suited the trade because a dense pressed piece carried well on long caravan routes. People care about Xiaguan because it is one of the few big names in pu’er from outside Xishuangbanna, so it stands for a different tradition from Menghai.

terms.gloss: Zhong Cha, the state tea company's mark

revisions.scope: The factory's change from state factory to joint-stock company to private owner, from the 1950s to the early 2000s. The year of private ownership is not covered.
revisions.text: After 1949 the factory came under the state tea company and, in the early 1950s, took the Zhong Cha mark that state factories used. In the mid 1950s the old private tea houses of Xiaguan were folded into it, and it settled into the name Yunnan Xiaguan Tea Factory. In the 1990s it was reorganised as a joint-stock company, and later it passed into private ownership. The year of that last step is given differently by different places and is not settled here. The effect for a buyer is that an older Xiaguan piece comes from the state factory era, while a newer one comes from a company, and the two should not be read as the same maker with the same record.

terms.gloss: iron cake, pressed hard under an iron press

revisions.scope: What sellers and drinkers commonly notice in Xiaguan raw pressed tea, especially iron cakes. A house tendency, never the taste of one lot.
revisions.text: Xiaguan’s raw pu’er has a name for a smoky edge. Sellers and drinkers most often mention it first, and a trade saying holds that Xiaguan without smoke is not Xiaguan. Its best known cakes are the iron cakes, pressed hard under an iron press into a dense disc with flat edges, and dense compression is part of why young Xiaguan is slow to open and can taste sharp or bitter. Many sellers say the smoke softens and the tea turns rounder and sweeter with years in storage, which is why older Xiaguan raw cakes are sought out. How much smoke a given cake shows, and how fast it fades, varies by year and by storage, and no agreed cause for the smoke is established.

revisions.scope: When Xiaguan began making ripe pu'er (the 1970s) and how it compares with Menghai. The comparison rests on a few sellers.
revisions.text: Xiaguan is known for raw pressed tea, but it also makes ripe pu’er. Wet piling reached the factory in the 1970s, the same years Kunming and Menghai took it up, and a ripe fermenting workshop was running by the middle of that decade. Accounts differ on the exact year, so only the decade is firm. A ripe Xiaguan from the 1990s therefore comes from a factory that had been making ripe tea for some years, and it is reasonable to expect a bolder, earthier ripe cup than the soft, sweet Menghai style, though that comparison rests on a few sellers only.

revisions.scope: What the Xiaguan name on a wrapper does and does not tell a buyer. Says the 'wild' line's definition is not established.
revisions.text: Xiaguan is a town and a maker. The name on a wrapper says where the tea was pressed and by whom. It does not by itself say where the leaf grew, how old the trees were, or what the recipe is. The factory has pressed raw and ripe tea, tuocha, bricks and cakes, under its own marks and under Zhong Cha, so a line such as a “wild” cake or an aged ripe brick has to be read from its own record. How the Xiaguan “wild” line is defined is not established: sellers use the words wild leaf or ancient wild tree on Xiaguan cakes, but no source read says what leaf stands behind the word. The place where Xiaguan sits, Dali, is covered on its own page.

terms.gloss: Ya'an, a city in western Sichuan

revisions.scope: Ya'an location and its place on the road to Tibet
revisions.text: Ya'an is a prefecture-level city in western Sichuan, on the western edge of the Sichuan Basin where the land climbs towards the Tibetan plateau. Mountains close it in, and four rivers run through it. It sits on the old road from the basin to Kangding and Tibet, which is why its tea went west. Mengding Shan, the best known tea mountain in Sichuan, is in Mingshan, in the east of the city's area.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

terms.gloss: Rain City, a nickname for Ya'an

revisions.scope: Why the climate suits tea around Ya'an
revisions.text: Ya'an is nicknamed the Rain City. Rain falls on most days of the year, the air stays damp and mist hangs on the hills, and the winters are mild because the mountains to the north shield it from cold air. Tea likes that: steady moisture, cloud cover and no hard frost. The hills around Mengding Shan are also heavily forested, and the soils are acidic yellow and red earths, which suit the tea bush.

terms.gloss: Ya'an Tibetan tea, the modern name for Sichuan border tea

revisions.scope: The two kinds of tea Ya'an is known for
revisions.text: Ya'an is known for two quite different kinds of tea. One is the green tea of Mengding Shan, made from young spring leaf and sold as a fine tea. The other is dark tea for Tibet, made from mature leaf and pressed into bricks. The city's tea trade today carries both names, Mengding Shan tea and Ya'an Tibetan tea. They share a place but not a market, a leaf grade or a way of drinking.

terms.gloss: Mengding sweet dew, a green tea
Mengding yellow bud, a yellow tea

revisions.scope: Mengding Shan and its teas
revisions.text: Mengding Shan is the mountain behind most of the fine tea of Ya'an. It rises to about 1,450 metres, and the tea gardens climb its slopes. Its best known teas are green: Mengding Ganlu, a small curled leaf, and Mengding Mao Feng and Shihua. It also makes a famous yellow tea, Mengding Huangya. The mountain's name is protected as a geographical indication, so Mengding Shan on a label should mean tea from this area. Tea tradition ties it to Wu Lizhen, said to have planted the first tea bushes here more than two thousand years ago. That is a story the trade tells with pride, and it is not proven history.

revisions.scope: Ya'an's role in the Tibet tea trade
revisions.text: For about a thousand years Ya'an was where tea for Tibet began its journey. Porters carried the bricks on foot from Ya'an to Kangding, and from there the tea went on to Lhasa and other Tibetan towns. In return Tibet sent horses. This is the reason Ya'an is a dark tea place as well as a green tea place. The making of that tea, the bricks and how they are drunk are on the page for Sichuan border tea.

revisions.scope: Zhenghe County in Nanping, northern Fujian: location and mountain setting. Altitude not stated.
revisions.text: Zhenghe is a county in the city of Nanping, in the north of Fujian. It is an inland mountain county, set back from the coast and covered in forest, with mist, cooler air and wider swings between day and night than the coastal tea hills. The trade points to that mountain setting when it explains why Zhenghe tea tastes the way it does. Altitude is quoted differently from place to place, so no single figure is given here. Tieshan is the township most often named in its tea story.

terms.gloss: Zhenghe Da Bai (Zhenghe big white tea)

revisions.scope: Zhenghe as a white tea county and its Zhenghe Da Bai bush. Not a claim about every tea labelled Zhenghe.
revisions.text: Zhenghe is one of the two main homes of white tea, with Fuding. It grows its own bush, Zhenghe Da Bai, a large-leaf variety with plump, downy buds. It buds later than the Fuding bushes and is usually described as the darker, taller-growing one. It is used for Silver Needle and White Peony, and it also makes black tea and a scented green tea. The bush is tied to Tieshan, where it is said to have been found in the late nineteenth century, and it is now planted well beyond the county.
revisions.reason: Approved by Claude on the Wisdom review page for Adrian, who asked Claude to decide (2026-11-27)

revisions.scope: The trade's general contrast between Zhenghe and Fuding white tea. A guide, not a rule for a single tea.
revisions.text: The trade sets Zhenghe against Fuding. Fuding is called the lighter, fresher, more floral style, and Zhenghe the fuller, rounder and mellower one, with a thicker liquor. Because Zhenghe leaf comes later in a rainy season, much of it is withered indoors, and some makers pile it longer, which adds to the deeper cup. This is the trade's comparison of two places and not a rule. Gardens, picking, processing and storage change a cup more than the county name does, and a few sellers reject the contrast altogether.

revisions.scope: Zhenghe Gongfu black tea as a style from the county. Dates and export history not covered.
revisions.text: Zhenghe also makes black tea. Zhenghe Gongfu is a Fujian gongfu black tea named for the county, and it is made from the same Da Bai bush as the white tea. It is counted among the classic Fujian black teas, alongside Bailin and Tanyang. It is described as a full, smooth, mellow cup with a sweet finish, and some sellers call it winey. The date it began and how widely it was exported are told differently from place to place and are not settled here.

revisions.scope: How Zhenghe's tea story is told. The county-name story is marked as unverified.
revisions.text: Zhenghe is an old tea county, and its name is part of the story. The usual telling says the emperor of the Song period renamed it after his reign title because he liked its tea. The tale is widely repeated, but it is copied from one page to the next and not checked against a record, so it is a story and not a fact on this page. What is better supported is the later one: the Da Bai bush was found and spread from Tieshan in the late nineteenth century, and Zhenghe white tea and black tea were both made for sale from about then.

Zhong Cha brand; the trademark of the China National Tea Corporation

revisions.scope: What the Zhong Cha Pai name means: a brand of the China National Tea Corporation, not a leaf grade. Applies to any tea sold under the mark.
revisions.text: Zhong Cha Pai means “Zhong Cha brand”. It is the name pu’er drinkers give to tea sold under the mark of the China National Tea Corporation, and it appears on ripe cakes, bricks and loose tea alike. It is a brand, not a grade of leaf: it says nothing about how fine or coarse the tea is, and it is not one of the leaf sorts that ripe pu’er is graded by. The company and its mark are covered on the China National Tea Corporation page.

terms.gloss: China Tea; short name of the China National Tea Corporation

revisions.scope: The two eras of the mark: state factories under the company until the 1980s, then newer and smaller makers licensed to use it. Applies to pu'er under the mark.
revisions.text: On a Zhong Cha tea, the year of manufacture tells you more than the mark does. Until the 1980s the big state factories made pu’er for the company, and the mark sat on teas that came out of one tightly run system. From the late 1980s the larger factories moved to their own names, and newer and smaller makers took up the Zhong Cha label, reportedly paying the company for the right. Two cakes with the same wrapper can therefore come from very different hands.

terms.gloss: ripe tea; the trade name for shou pu'er

revisions.scope: Ripe pu'er under the mark can date only from the 1970s on; most met today are from the 1990s on. Applies to ripe (shou) pu'er sold under the mark.
revisions.text: Ripe pu’er only began in the 1970s, so any ripe cake under the mark is from that decade or later. Most ripe Zhong Cha cakes people meet today date from the 1990s onward, the time when the label was being used by many makers, so the page for the mark cannot say how a particular ripe cake will taste. That depends on the factory, the recipe and how the cake has been stored.

terms.gloss: inner ticket pressed into a cake

revisions.scope: What buyers check beyond the wrapper on a Zhong Cha tea, and the caution about copies. Applies to pu'er under the mark.
revisions.text: Buyers who know the mark check more than the outer paper. The inner ticket and the insert, the recipe code where there is one, and whether the stated year fits that recipe all help to place a cake. Wrappers often leave out the year, and the leaf is hard to trace, so a seller’s record of where the cake has been matters. Zhong Cha is also among the most copied pu’er names, and an old date is easy to claim, so a very low price for a tea said to be old is a reason to ask more.
